I should like to ask why it is not possible to enumerate the particular classes to which the amendment is applied, instead of putting it in the form in which we have it in tariff items 1215 and 1216, namely, an exemption from the provisions of these items by regulation of the governor in council in any particular case or class of cases.
The explanatory note gives a number of examples to which the proposed amendment is intended to apply, such as automobiles acquired by Canadians returning to Canada, and so forth. If this purports to be a complete enumeration of the classes of cases to which it is intended the amendment shall apply, why could we not have the classes set out in items 1215 and 1216 instead of clothing the governor in council with the power to make exemptions?

subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO USED OR SECONDHAND MOTOR VEHICLES AND AIRCRAFT
speechtext:
There is no great uniformity in the cases that will come up for consideration with reference to import into Canada of used cars or used aircraft. There are now 170 applications before the customs department, including 129 passenger cars, 24 trucks, 4 buses, a motorcycle and an ambulance. The reasons for the applications are many and varied. Some of them might be called distress cases, others compassionate cases, still others are for business reasons.
The applications as to 48 of the cars and trucks indicate that they were for gifts to Canadians from friends or relatives in the United States. Thirty-eight were from relatives, and of these, thirty-five were from immediate relatives-that is, father, mother, brother, son or daughter. Gifts of used cars by friends totalled 10; of these, three were donations to religious workers in

Canada-gifts from religious groups or orders to Canadian evangelistic or religious orders, the parent body of which was in the United States.
There are also a number of cases of gifts from immediate relatives where the prohibition is particularly harsh. For instance, an American girl whose health has been poor married a Canadian. Her father wishes to give her one of the two family cars to facilitate her transportation and that of her family. Another case concerns a brother whose sister and her husband operate a small store. The brother is a successful businessman in the United States, and he wishes to donate a small truck.
A number of cases which should receive favourable consideration have to do with students. Twenty-three of the applications were from students who are taking postgraduate or specialized courses, and who resided in a foreign country for one to three years. Several of them were operating on D.V.A. subsidies, and they wish to have the car to save travelling expenses in moving their families, and to keep it for use in Canada.
Some real cases of hardship were created by the prohibition. The department's only alternative was to permit temporary entry into Canada which would be on a six months' permit. This meant that at the end of that time the car had to be exported and sold, causing great inconvenience and financial loss.
With regard to workers, nineteen workers who had obtained employment in the United States bought cars to transport them back and forth to work. They wished to bring them into Canada for reasons similar to those given by the students. The difference between these two classes is largely in the length of time the person was in the foreign country, the student being bound to at least one year, while the worker may stay for a period of only one month.
There is also the problem of tourists. Eight Canadian tourists who had acquired cars while visiting other countries wish to bring the cars back with them. The practice of buying a car in England for the purpose of touring the United Kingdom and Europe has been growing, and will probably become a greater attraction because of the devaluation of the pound. A problem arises when a Canadian purchases a car abroad and returns to Canada the next year. Such a car, having been manufactured prior to the year of importation, is therefore prohibited entry.
Customs Tariff
I could go on and enumerate many cases of distress. Take the matter of school busses. Every hon. member knows that the consolidation of schools necessitates the use of busses in a large number of rural areas. Some of these communities are not in a financial position to purchase new busses, but they can get used busses in the United States at a reasonable price, and thus give service to the community and to the school section at considerably less cost.
With reference to the importation of used aircraft and cars, it should be understood that the normal rate of duty still applies, and an appraisal value is put upon the used vehicle by the appraisers of the customs department.
One cannot set up a standard or uniform basis on which these vehicles will be allowed entry into this country; the cases must be considered on their individual merits. It is for this reason that we ask the house to give the minister and his officials the power to make application to the governor in council to permit entry of such vehicles in particular cases.

subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO USED OR SECONDHAND MOTOR VEHICLES AND AIRCRAFT
speechtext: Undoubtedly the minister has made out a case for entry of the vehicles of the kinds he has mentioned and in the circumstances to which he has referred. The concern of the committee must be with the way in which it is proposed to meet the situation, namely, by giving power to the governor in council to promulgate regulations in particular cases or classes of cases. From the concluding remarks of the minister I gather that the department has given consideration to the possibility of enumerating the classes of cases in items 1215 and 1216, and has found it impossible to make an effective or exhaustive enumeration. This leads one to the conclusion that most of the cases are to be handled by individual orders in council rather than by regulations applying to classes of cases. To the end that there may be some measure of parliamentary control, I think we should ask the minister whether reports will be made to the house on the cases in which the power conferred by this bill is exercised.

speechtext: Where citizens of the United States have tourist camps or summer businesses in Canada, most of them come in with their cars under tourist's permit; but I understand that if they bring a car, a station wagon or a truck, they cannot use it in connection with their business in Canada. I am afraid that items 1215 and 1216 are going to have a most serious effect. The minister may shake his head, but they are going to have an injurious effect on Canadian industry. What are you getting in exchange for these concessions? You are going to repeal two items in the Customs Tariff, and substitute for them items 1215 and 1216. What will be the effect? We used to have a large trade in automobiles with Australia, New Zealand and other places. At the present time trade and commerce and industry are not getting as many orders, with the result that a large number of people are out of work. In this country we used to have what is called preferential trade with Britain and the dominions. We had trade with the old country on these items. Now you have lost your best customer in many products to which I will not refer today.
This provision applies to used or secondhand automobiles and motor vehicles of all kinds manufactured prior to the calendar year in which importation into Canada is sought to be made. Then there is reference to automobiles given to religious institutions or clergy engaged in religious or welfare work; trucks and aircraft imported as part of the equipment of United States firms engaged in exploratory or development work in the Alberta oil fields. Something might be said in favour of that, but this type of aircraft is not available in Canada for use in prospecting or in the transportation of supplies to remote areas. I fail to see how it is going to aid Canadian industry, because if there ever was a time when the small wholesale or retail man and the small manufacturer wanted help it is now, when taxation is at the peak. We used to spend $36 million on the whole civil government; now we are spending almost that much a day. We have got away up in the clouds-in the billions. I fail to see how this is going to help the manufacturer, small or large, who goes in for this type of work. If you ask me, it is going to have a very serious effect on industry generally throughout Canada.

speechtext: That shows what parliament can do.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND INCOME WAR TAX ACT AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
This bill has been before the house and available to hon. members for some three weeks, and the announcement has been before the public for some six months. I find that in most other groups, long before parliament attempts to discuss any proposed measure the people who are interested come to the department for information, or put in briefs, or make suggestions as to changes which should be made. It greatly facilitates the work of parliament if they do that sort of thing. I am not criticizing anyone for failing to do it. I am simply stating as a fact that the only representations that were made that this new system would adversely affect the farming group were made in the committee last night. I do not believe that it will. I think that when the farming community understand the basis on which it operates; when they understand that if they overdepreciate, it must be put back, but that, conversely, if they underdepreciate they can get the benefit of the law as a result of underdepreciation, they will come to the conclusion that the new system is better than the old one.
Be that as it may, there is no desire to force the system on the farming community. I can see that it might be difficult for farmers who have not complete records to keep track of the diminishing value, the diminishing balance basis; but bigger farmers would have no difficulty at all. Perhaps the smaller ones who keep their books less carefully would have some difficulty, and, having become accustomed to the straight-line basis, would prefer to keep it. I am not prepared to accept the view that the farmer as such is any more obtuse than any other member of the community; but in any event so far as the department is concerned there is no objection to the farming community continuing for the time being to operate their depreciation on the straight-line basis. It may be that after they have seen how it works for others they will prefer to have a new basis. Be that as it may, I have no objection to farmers and fishermen, who are both given special treatment under the act, as the committee knows, by being allowed to average over five years, continuing to depreciate on the same basis as that which has been followed in the past. To this end I have a simple amendment to section 7 which provides that subsection 1, which relates to

Income Tax Act
the so-called recapture provision, shall not apply to farmers and fishermen. Under the regulations the basis for depreciation in the case of farmers will be the base period, as in the past, namely, the straight-line basis.

Representations have been made by the Toronto board of trade in connection with subsection 3 which deals with nonresident owned investment corporations The board states:
The board has interpreted the provisions of the Income War Tax Act as extending the dividend exemption of section 4(n) to nonresident-owned investment corporations. The proposed legislation appears to be a retroactive change denying the exemption referred to. The board has on many occasions urged that retroactive tax legislation be not resorted to, and again points out that in the opinion of the board this is a highly undesirable practice and should be avoided.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND INCOME WAR TAX ACT AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
As my hon. friend knows, this section relates to a relatively small number of companies owned by nonresidents who have investments in Canada. In 1946 they were given a special basis of tax treatment. They are taxed on the earnings of the company, not at the full corporation rate but at a special rate. Prior to 1946 it used to be 22J- per cent, with a deduction of 7J per cent on income received from dividends on Canadian taxpaying corporations. In 1946 that technical difference was eliminated and the straight rate was made 15 per cent. However by inadvertence the provision of the corresponding tax credit section was not amended. If this section were not put in, the

nonresident would in fact be getting a tax credit to which he was not entitled, which has never been allowed by the department, and for which I do not think there is any justification, in equity or otherwise.
Technically it is true that the effect of this section is to take the amendment back to 1946 when the change from 22J per cent to 15 per cent was made, as I have indicated. I do not think any real objection can be taken to it.

subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND INCOME WAR TAX ACT AMENDMENTS
speechtext: Would there be any serious loss if the section were made effective from the date of the minister's budgetary pronouncement? This would obviate any suggestion of unfairness resulting from the retroactivity of taxing legislation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND INCOME WAR TAX ACT AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
I do not think so. I have before me the text of the resolution introduced in April 1946, which states:
That the special rates provided for nonresident-owned investment corporations be reduced for the 1947 and subsequent taxation years from 221 per cent to 15 per cent, but that such corporations be taxable on all income received in Canada subject to deductions from the said income in respect of interest and dividends received from other such corporations and foreign taxes paid by the corporation.
In other words, the rate having been reduced from 22J per cent to 15 per cent, there should not have been and there was never intended to be a tax credit to offset that 7J per cent. The old system was 22J per cent and a tax credit of 7i per cent, coming from a certain type of investment. Having consolidated the two and taken the straight 15 per cent rate, as indicated in the resolution, the tax credit was to be eliminated. Through some oversight the tax credit section was not amended. But no nonresident-owned investment corporation has ever asserted that it should in fairness get the tax credit. They have never been allowed it. This is simply to cover the oversight in the drafting of the law. There is no justifiable claim for this tax credit.

I received a letter, dated November 29, 1949, from the Newfoundland board of trade, which reads:
I have been directed to bring to your attention that part of the income tax bill at present before the federal house which has reference to Newfoundland's special position under the terms of union.
It seems clear from clause 48, subclause 3, that business losses prior to confederation will not be allowable as deductions from profits made after union when computing taxable income. In other words, section 28, paragraph (d), of the Canadian Income Tax Act will not apply to Newfoundland taxpayers before April 1, 1949. Clause 48, subclause 3, of the bill reads as follows:
Clause 48, subclause 3, of the bill now under consideration is then quoted, and the letter continues:
On the other hand there appears to be no provision in the bill which will relieve Newfoundland taxpayers from income tax and surtax upon dividends paid out of profits earned before union with Canada.
Further, there seems to be no provision in the bill which will prevent section 9, subsection 6, of the Canadian act being applied to individual shareholders. This subsection provides that if the undivided profits of a corporation exceed what is reasonably required for the purposes of the business, a dividend equal to the amount specified by the minister shall be deemed to have been received by the shareholders. This may result in substantial taxes becoming payable upon pre-confederation profits.
A refusal to allow the carrying forward of preconfederation losses on the one hand and to impose tax upon dividends from profits before union on the other hand seems grossly inequitable.
Yours faithfully,
H. T. Renouf,
Secretary.
Perhaps the minister could make a statement with regard to the taxation picture as it affects Newfoundland and clear up some of the points brought out in this letter.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND INCOME WAR TAX ACT AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
The hon. member will recall that under the terms of union with Newfoundland, or the supplementary agreement,
[Mr. Abbott.!
it was a condition that taxes would not be imposed with respect to either personal or corporation income tax in Newfoundland on earnings prior to the date of union; that in effect they would be given the same treatment as was given in Canada when the pay-as-you-go plan was adopted. The representatives of Newfoundland in the discussions were insistent that we should not look behind the date of union as to the position of a taxpayer in Newfoundland, and may I say at once that I have no quarrel with that position.
My hon. friend has raised two points, the first being with respect to the fact that losses incurred prior to the date of union would not be taken into account in subsequent years when the Newfoundland taxpayer is taxed in Canada. That is correct. Obviously when one is not entitled to look at profits in previous years, one cannot very well look at losses; the one must go with the other. So far as the income tax payer in Canada is concerned, I suppose the Newfoundland taxpayer can be looked upon as a newborn babe. We do not inquire into his tax status before he became a Canadian citizen.
As to undistributed surpluses on hand at the date of union, the same treatment is accorded here as was accorded to the Canadian taxpayer who first became liable for income tax in 1917. Under the law as it stands, pre-1917 surpluses can be distributed on liquidation free of income tax. Dividends are taxable income by definition under the law, and we do not look to see where a dividend comes from. That is true of dividends declared by any Canadian corporation. A pre-confederation surplus of a Newfoundland corporate taxpayer can be carried on its books and when distributed on winding up, or by any other method other than dividend payments, can be so distributed free of tax.

speechtext: The section is based on the legal view, if you like, that technically international agreements, fisheries agreements or the bases agreements and that sort of thing in Newfoundland, are not automatically subject to Canadian legislation, but that we must extend our legislation to those agreements. This provision is inserted for that purpose. Probably my hon. friend knows that there are fishing agreements and fishing rights in connection with the old colony of Newfoundland that go back a great many years, and this section is inserted in order to make sure that we can take appropriate action to continue the international effect of those agreements and their adoption by Canada. speakeroldname: Hon. R. W. Mayhew (Minister of Fisheries):
speechtext:
Before the committee proceeds with consideration of the items in the estimates, Mr. Chairman, I should like to give to the committee a statement and a report.
Since coming into this department approximately eighteen months ago I have, with some of the departmental staff, visited each of the ten provinces to discuss fisheries problems, prospects and betterment. These discussions have been held with provincial government officials, processors, fishermen, wholesalers, and cold storage and warehouse interests.
Supply-Fisheries
With each, the conversations were on their own problems, but, where possible, joint discussions also took place. Our visits took us from Bonavista, on the east side of Newfoundland, to Ucluelet, on the west side of Vancouver island.
These trips were for the purpose of gathering information for a composite picture of the whole industry, yet as intimate a picture as possible of the different districts. I therefore feel I should report on what the departmental officers and I have learned about this industry, and to give the committee also some idea of the actions we think we should take on behalf of the industry.
The fishing industry is North America's oldest industry. It is still a growing one, too. In the past thirty years, British Columbia production has doubled, as it has also in western Nova Scotia. In Newfoundland and the other areas around the gulf of St. Lawrence it has grown somewhat less.
In some east coast areas, the industry has been unable to provide good living standards for fishermen, except during the two great wars. Now, following the war, some of the eastern districts are again in a weak position. These weak spots stand in contrast to our great fishing resources. Canada has access to the world's greatest fishery resources on the Atlantic and the Pacific. We have the largest inland fresh-water fishery in the world. But on our east coast we do not fully use the available resources, although many foreign vessels catch fish right up to our coastal limits. On our Pacific coast the industry takes all the salmon, halibut and herring allowable without destroying the stocks. On the east coast, however, apart from a few species, such as lobster and Atlantic salmon, the resource is underdeveloped. The fish are there, and so are the fishermen; yet many fishermen have a poor living. Hon. members will want me to try to explain this condition.
In the first place fish are very perishable, as perishable as milk. But the fishing industry has to sell its products hundreds or even thousands of miles from the sea. Canned fish, it is true, may be shipped to grocery stores all over the world. But fresh, frozen, smoked or salted products suffer rapid spoilage.
Most of the finest things in the world are delicate. "Delicious" and "delicate" are almost the same word. They go together; and that is true of fish.
While fresh and frozen fish are difficult to merchandise, the methods are improving daily. The chain of refrigeration from the coast to the shops and to the housewives'

Supply-Fisheries
kitchens is steadily growing. The fish product in modem packaged form is becoming more and more attractive. As a result, market expansion is possible.
Our fish trade has been held back, particularly on the east coast and in Newfoundland, by continued dependence on the traditional product-salted fish. Likewise it depends on traditional markets in the Mediterranean countries and the West Indies, where salted cod has to be sold to buyers whose capacity to pay is limited. However, some companies have switched away from salted fish to the fresh and frozen forms. These find their market in North America, where consumers' living standards are higher. The fresh and frozen products require more careful handling, but they are likely to yield greater and more stable financial returns in the future.
Processing-filleting, packaging and freezing-calls for larger plants using more up-to-date methods. In British Columbia this development took place readily. In the modern plants of Newfoundland and western Nova Scotia it is already well advanced, and in Gaspe, too-although Gaspe suffers from having only a five-months season.
Elsewhere on the Atlantic coast the future will see the concentration of industry at fewer ports, where modern processing and modern fishing methods will ensure more adequate living for fishermen. I shall return to this problem later.
You see a striking contrast between the development of agriculture and that of fisheries in the past forty years. Behind agriculture's progress goes quite a big national effort. Hon. members know the work of the federal Department of Agriculture in its science services, its production and market services, its experimental farms and demonstration stations. Alongside are the efforts of the provinces, both in research and demonstration, and the work of agricultural colleges. But in fisheries our national effort has been small in all these services. In the federal government our job up to 1938 was mainly the conservation of fish stocks. Only recently work has begun on fish inspection and the like. We still lack demonstration services to fishermen, as we have in agriculture.
For all these reasons some of our fishery resources have been under-used, our domestic and North American markets have not been built up, and we have areas of low standards in many of our fishing communities.
So far I have been talking about our coastal fisheries. Somewhat similar problems face the inland fisheries. Today I want to

outline the future government program for meeting these problems. Some work has been started, and I should like to mention it first.
In British Columbia, which I mention first for no special reason, the fishing industry has expanded near the limit of the available fish resources. On that coast, therefore, the departmental program has a different emphasis from that in the east. In the west the need is partly for adequate protection of the stocks; and since the war we have increased the number of protective officers and boats to help meet this problem. But of more positive value are the steps being taken to expand the stocks of the valuable species. Such expansion calls for new methods of river management, for improvement of lakes through control of predators, for control of pollution, and in some cases for use of fish culture and hatcheries. This work is expanding in a new division of the department, made up of engineers and biologists.
Here, I might add, we intend to do everything necessary to conserve the salmon resource of British Columbia. We are anxious, however, to co-operate with those interested in hydro development. The department believes fish conservation and industrial growth can proceed without undue restraint on either side.
In the inland areas the direct responsibility of the federal government is in the Northwest Territories. Research has begun on the life history and spawning habits of goldeye, Arctic char and the beluga. A research vessel, the Calanus, has been sent to Arctic waters, and exploration at Great Slave lake has in recent years helped establish a new commercial fishery.
To help the fishery in the inland provinces, an inspection system for whitefish was introduced and is being currently expanded. The federal government is working along with the prairie provinces in research into the conditions affecting the fresh-water fisheries.
On the east coast, as in British Columbia, attention has been given to raising the supplies of the valuable species for which there appears to be always a ready market, such as lobster, Atlantic salmon, oysters, and clams. New research work has been undertaken in the scallop, flounder, salmon and shrimp fisheries. To help raise the standards, demonstrations of new fishing techniques are being carried out in flounder dragging, Danish seining, the Larsen floating trawl, and long-lining. This work of the St. Andrews station has already brought changes in fishing methods, and in the regulations issued by the department for conservation needs. On this coast, too, the department has increased its staff of

protective officers, as well as its patrol fleet -as for example the launching of a new 65-foot vessel last month in Shelburne.
Research at Grand river and Halifax stations has expanded in recent years. To help develop the fresh and frozen trade, intensive studies have been made of the problems affecting the keeping qualities of fish, with results that are internationally recognized. New methods of controlling bacteria on boats and in processing have produced striking benefits to the industry. So has the development of salt fish dryers, smokers and machines for washing, cleaning and cutting fish for the expanding frozen fish trade.
Most of the industrial firms in the east are small, and depend for research entirely on the federal government. Only by finding new ways of doing old jobs, or by doing new things, is progress possible. The benefits of this research are evident particularly in southwestern Nova Scotia.
In Newfoundland the terms of union gave the federal government certain responsibilities for the administration of fisheries and the bait service. The integration into the federal government of these services has been completed. In addition, the Newfoundland fisheries board, whose powers now relate to salted fish, is being continued for five years after union. The union of Newfoundland with Canada adds greatly to our stature as a fishing country.
These various steps show what has been done to further the development of Canada's fisheries.
Before outlining our future program I should like to say a few words about the fisheries prices support board. Since its origin in 1947 the board has twice given price support, once in the maritimes and once in the prairie provinces. These two actions were reasonably satisfactory in bringing immediate relief to the fishermen concerned. But the expenditures provided no constructive longterm solution of the basic problems of the fisheries.
Fortunately, despite the loss of many important markets in Europe and in the sterling area, the industry so far has been able to meet most of its difficulties. Serious or widespread price collapse has been avoided. However, some operations have faced and suffered loss.
Prices support legislation alone cannot solve the whole problem. Prices support is a stopgap solution to meet emergencies. It cannot remove all the hindrances to expansion I mentioned earlier. And these cause low income to fishermen. We believe that the support act is necessary as a short-term measure, but a constructive program must be
Supply-Fisheries
found to remove the basic troubles. More fundamental remedies are to be found in better organization and methods in the fishing industry, both in producing and in selling. Future prosperity on a continuing, steady basis depends on marketing better quality products, both at home and abroad.
A proposal along these lines was made last May, and later discussed with the fishing industry at meetings in all the provinces. In September the fisheries council met in Ottawa, and gave the government its views on the proposals. I wish now to present to the committee the program we have drawn up.
This program might better be termed a framework for fishery development. It is aimed at removing the hindrances to expansion. Responsibility for its successful application, however, cannot rest alone on the government. We shall expect from industry a full measure of co-operation. On its part, industry must assume its rightful share of the risks as well as the rewards, and in doing so it will show initiative, and I might even say courage, far greater than at any time in the past.
Broadly speaking, future fisheries development probably lies in two directions: (1) in the expansion of North American and overseas markets; and (2) in the development of backward areas, which are primarily in the east but found also in the inland provinces. I should like to deal first with market expansion.
Hon. members will agree with me, I think, that quality determines quantity; that you cannot build a good turnover unless you have a good product. This is true in any trade, but it is especially true for fish. It is quality that sells. Now, getting good quality is not simply a matter of inspection of the product or the plant. Government inspection is only one of the steps. I want to say here how pleased I am that our fish inspection bill has received such warm support from members on both sides of the house. This bill will give us a chance to build an effective inspection service within the department, whereby inspection can be carried out in boats and plants and through the wholesale and retail trades.
But there must be more than inspection. Quality depends on how fish is handled in boats, in plants, in the selling trades-yes, and in the kitchens of restaurants and homes. From sea to table is a long assembly line; each part must do its own job well, but each has to fit into the other. Any program must cover each of these steps and try to provide for the industry the conditions that will allow it to do each of the jobs better.

Supply-Fisheries
The market expansion should be sought first, I believe, in North America. With us fish consumption is low, and the chances of greatly increasing our sales are excellent. To this end our program will be in three phases. There will be the extension of fish inspection, which will require a new division within the Department of Fisheries. The second part of the program will cover the assembly line I have already mentioned. We propose to establish another division within the present department, a division of technical services. The object here is to provide fishermen, small plants, and the wholesale and retail trade, with technical help in the improvement of their individual operations. This service would be advisory and would require able and qualified technical personnel. We believe it to be basic, and perhaps even more helpful than inspection for the over-all improvement in quality. We believe also that the provision and use of such a service should be prior to any extensive campaigns of advertising fishery products.
Without expanding on this at the moment we hope to add a third smaller division to the department in the form of a consumer services branch to work in the field of consumer education.
These three new services will be available for the Canadian fishing industry as a whole, although of course special emphasis will have to be laid on the technical development of the backward areas.
In market expansion these new services may be expected to operate as follows:
One section of the new technical services division will probably be devoted to the distributive outlets, giving to wholesalers and retailers in the main Canadian cities the knowledge, developed and approved through research, at home and abroad, that is necessary for better fish-handling. While this service will help to overcome some problems, it may not be sufficient to create the desired retail facilities. More direct steps of a financial nature are not being considered, since we hope that the industry and manufacturers of refrigeration equipment will help finance the extended use of low-cost freezing equipment.
Adequate railway transportation, especially on long hauls, is vital to the successful distribution of fish in North America. Our scientists have played a full part in discovering means of improving such facilities. We now intend to make every effort to encourage both railway companies to use and test the new type of refrigerator car that has been provided, and that can be
[Mr. Mayhew.l
used not only for fish but for other perishable foods as well. One of our own staff, Mr. Young, is responsible for this equipment.
I cannot deal with distribution without taking into account the export market. The position of some parts of the industry remains crucial and may even deteriorate further. Newfoundland and British Columbia have always leaned heavely on European and commonwealth markets, while the maritimes, in their salt fish trade, have depended on the markets of the West Indies. It is vitally important, therefore, that any general policies that look forward to the opening of such markets or to reduction in United States tariffs should give fullest consideration to the fish trade, and this the government will endeavour to do.
To round out the first phase of our new program, we plan to extend our work in the field of consumer education, as already mentioned. As some hon. members are aware, we now have available a new experimental kitchen. There, under the direction of trained home economists, fish products will be tested and new recipes created. These home economists will also be assigned to field duties, where they will give demonstrations and lectures on fish cooking to women's groups and to schools.
We intend also to develop relationships with those responsible for institutional feeding, with chefs of railways, hotels and restaurants. Not only shall we endeavour to encourage greater use of fish in mass feeding, but we shall also provide for this purpose as many technical services as possible.
To supplement this work we plan to develop new educational aids that will help consumers to know how to buy, what to buy, and how to cook and how to serve fish. We are planning new cookbooks, new pamphlets, instructional films and exhibitions.
The creation of these new services to the industry and consumers cannot be achieved overnight; we have no large industry, no large fishery schools from which to draw staff. Personnel will have to be trained, and some years will pass before the full benefits are evident to all. The important thing is to launch the program now, and to look for new hope and new progress throughout the industry in the next five years.
I now come to phase two of our program, that which concerns the development of backward areas. The administration of the fisheries in some provinces-the inland provinces and Quebec-is left by arrangement to the provincial governments. In the other provinces the federal government has complete responsibility for fisheries matters.

Because of this the department is considering the advisability of calling a conference with the provinces for review of joint action in the areas experiencing difficulty. Meanwhile the following steps will be taken by the federal government:
Earlier in this statement I referred to the underdevelopment of the east coast fishery resources. Accordingly, to help the industry of the maritimes take greater advantage of the stocks available, and at the same time to help them meet market demands for fresh and frozen fish, we have reviewed our policy in connection with Atlantic coast fishing trawlers.
At present licences for trawlers are issued only to Canadian-built ships. It has now been decided that licences will be granted to new trawlers built in the United Kingdom as well as in Canadian yards. Licences will be issued also to the better types of secondhand trawlers, bought either in the United States or in the United Kingdom, and registered in Canada after the payment of duty. Licences, however, will be granted to companies obtaining a secondhand trawler only when that company has laid down a new keel in Canada. These steps will help the east coast fishing industry modernize their fishing operations at somewhat lower costs than before, and the trawlers themselves will help to stabilize supplies and maintain quality and variety of fish foods.
In the backward areas, as already mentioned, there is a special need for the establishment of technical and demonstration services to fishermen and to small plants, particularly in the maritimes and in Newfoundland. These services are as necessary to fisheries as experimental farms and demonstration stations are to agriculture. We plan, accordingly, to use the new technical services division to demonstrate in each of the main fishing areas the best that is known on fishing and fish handling methods. We propose also to develop an intelligence service to fishermen, one of the most important functions of which would be to advise on the whereabouts of fish schools during the various seasons. Some additional staff will be required by the department carry out this work, and there will be need for the acquisition or chartering of demonstration fishing vessels and gear.
The recovery of the poorer fishery areas in the east may require more than technical guidance.
We know we have to extend greatly our exploration and our surveys of the fish stocks around these coasts, and this too is part of our program. When you go to many of these communities you get the impression that they
Supply-Fisheries
may be submarginal, that there is just not enough fish locally available to give the men a decent living. But you cannot be sure; so many of these communities depend on very small boats that can fish only a few miles from shore. Their equipment is so poor that they have to wait on the fish coming, to them. With better equipment they would fish further afield, and go where the fish happen to be. We are not always sure, however, where fish are to be found, and in what numbers. The survey of the sea is not like making soil surveys. It is more difficult, more expensive, and takes longer to produce results.
I am sure, however, that greater exploration of our fish stocks is necessary-necessary in helping fishermen, and in helping to decide what areas are really submarginal, and what areas merit new investment in the form of harbours, boats, and plants. Much survey work will be necessary to give us the facts on which to reach decisions of value.
There are of course, in some parts of the east, other industrial problems beyond fisheries. The future expansion of the fishery has to be part of a more general program, and the success of such development will depend on the closest liaison between the federal and provincial governments. Each has an important part to play. Likewise the fishing industry itself has a major responsibility. Some parts of the industry may lack the management or the capital necessary for prosperous expansion. This we shall be surveying carefully. But I am convinced that the east has management, and much available capital, too, ready to apply to the expansion. At present there is a hesitation caused by the need to turn to new methods and new products. That hesitation, I am equally convinced, will give place to forceful action as the possibilities within the North American market reveal themselves. After all, if the people of North America each ate one pound of fish more per year, the fishing industry could hardly begin to meet the demand. The future is bright. The resource is there, and if not fully used by Canadians, will be further controlled by other countries.
The program I have outlined can begin now. The new services in inspection, in the technical application of scientific knowledge to fish production and selling, in consumer services, and in the greater exploration of the seas and its valuable species, will all aid market expansion. As it proceeds, the more backward areas can, by federal and provincial action, move in on the new developments.
The estimates now before the committee are of course those prepared a year ago. The new program will begin to be reflected in next year's estimates.

I want to congratulate the minister on the wonderful address he has given us on our fisheries.
It is one o'clock, Mr. Chairman.
At one o'clock the committee took recess.
The committee resumed at three o'clock.

When the committee rose at one o'clock, Mr. Chairman, I had just said grace before luncheon by offering my thanks and congratulations to the Minister of Fisheries. I had in mind making some extended remarks myself, but in view of the minister's address, in which he presented the over-all picture so well, I am going to make my remarks quite brief.
Prior to the election last June, the government, through the Prime Minister and the Minister of Fisheries, announced its policies on several occasions. I might say that those policies, and the way they were announced, did not meet with the approval of the fishermen, the fisheries or even myself. It is understandable that they would not suit me. In announcing their policies, both the Prime Minister and the Minister of Fisheries enumerated them in detail, and they always commenced with these words: "The government should do this," or "the government should do that." What we needed at that time was to have a little "will" put into it. I should have liked to see the announcement read, "The government will do this or that for the benefit of the fishermen." I hope the Minister of Fisheries will put that thought into action, so that instead of hearing him say, "My government should do this," I shall hear him say, "My government will do this in the interests of the fisheries."
Some time ago there was a full day's debate on fisheries in this house. At that time the members from the different provinces across Canada extolled the fisheries of their provinces. If I were to go into that in detail today, I would be only repeating what was said at that time. I might say this, however, that in the province of Prince Edward Island from which I come, we have without doubt, and without making any apologies to anybody, the finest fish that are caught. The fishermen are looking for broader and better markets for their fish. This is one of the most important things we shall have to consider.
For some of our products, such as lobsters, oysters, and a few others, we find a ready market at paying prices. For the canned fish and fresh fish, we have practically no market outside our own province. If the minister will fulfil that one part of his policy, namely,
[Mr. Mayhew.l
the bringing into use of refrigerator cars for transporting fresh fish, and also the establishing of refrigerated stores in some of the large centres, then I believe he will have accomplished something for the fishing industry.
As I said a moment ago, it is not my intention to make extended remarks, but while I am speaking on this vote No. 101, departmental administration, I wish to say that these estimates have been brought down in the usual way. I regret, Mr. Chairman, that the same antiquated ideas prevail, except in the case of the estimates' of the Department of National Defence. The committee is being asked to vote approximately $7,200,000 for the carrying out of the work of the Department of Fisheries. Details are given for about 75 per cent of that amount, and then we are asked to vote a blank cheque for about $1,650,000. There are 47 permanent civil servants listed, the payment for whom amounts to $153,620. Temporary services in the same department cost $146,280. The details are given for the expenditure concerning the permanent civil servants, such as the amount each one receives, the position and grade, and so on. When it comes to temporary employees, we do not know whether there are 50, 60, or 100.
My first question of the minister is to give us some details with respect to this additional blank cheque which he is asking this committee to vote. I may say further in connection with this, that there is always a suspicion in the minds of most of us, although it is not voiced by the members on the government side. What else is covered in this vote of $146,280 in addition to the wages for temporaries?
