Mr. Chairman, I am sure that all those interested in

the fishing industry will be pleased by the statement made by the Minister of Fisheries this morning. He dealt with this oldest industry in its various stages, and finished by stating that the industry is still growing. I like that "still growing" because I believe there is plenty of opportunity for this industry to develop to a great extent. He referred to the activities of the agriculture department. We who have followed the agricultural activities as compared with the fisheries believe we understand just what the minister meant. Perhaps the greatest piece of legislation in connection with advancement similar to that made in agriculture was the recent introduction of that bill entitled the "Fish Inspection Act". The members from the maritimes discussed this bill, and we were indeed pleased at the reception it met with from all groups in the house. I was particularly impressed with the able manner in which the hon. member for Queens-Shelbume dealt with this Fish Inspection Act. While I do not propose to go over all the points raised by him, in fairness to our section of the country I felt that I should once again bring to the attention of the maritimes one or two points raised by him.
He paid a deserving tribute to the fisher-folk of his particular part of Nova Scotia, in pointing out that during the years when things were not as good as they are now in Canada and the rest of the world, namely in the thirties, they by their industrious habits and manner of taking care of themselves did not look for relief but rather went out and through their own efforts raised sufficient vegetables and other things for the household-even by the planting of small gardens on the rockbound coast of Nova Scotia-and were thus able to carry on without any help from the so-called relief fund.
He also touched on what I thought was an important development in Nova Scotia, particularly in his part of the province, when he referred to the processing of kelp. He told us how this was not only used in his own province but was exported to Rockland, Maine, where various drugs and compounds were derived from it and were sold all over the United States. I think the picture he painted with regard to the fisheries industry as it applies to the province of Nova Scotia, and particularly to his own constituency, was exceptionally well received, because I have had many letters stating how pleased the writers were that our new member from Queens-Shelburne had taken such an active part and shown such a keen interest in this particular subject. I thought that it was only fair, Mr. Chairman, that I should pay that
Supply-Fisheries
tribute today because of the fine picture painted by the minister in his report to us this morning. The two of them will, I think, be well worth preserving and reading in future.
Perhaps you will wonder, Mr. Chairman, why I departed a little bit from the subject.
I would judge from the nod of your head and the wonderment on your face that you were about to say "Come back to the subject." It is all part of the picture of the fisheries industry. That was perhaps the first chapter. Then the second chapter was as developed by the minister this morning in his remarks. He covered the ground fully and gave us the program or framework as to the future of his department. I was indeed pleased to know that he had taken a broad view of this picture and that he was not going to allow it to stand still as it has done to a certain extent in the past. Perhaps it is because we have a combination of interests in the minister and the parliamentary assistant. In the minister we have one from the extreme west who is looking after the interests of the fishing industry as it pertains to the west and to the rest of Canada; and with him as parliamentary assistant he has an exceedingly able man from the province of Prince Edward Island. We therefore have one of the extreme eastern provinces and one of the extreme western provinces represented in the combination that exists today.
I think I should also pay a compliment to the efficient organization we now have in the Department of Fisheries. Our deputy minister is one whose reputation is known throughout Canada and the United States, and his name is well known overseas also. Hence I say that we are today in a more fortunate position perhaps than ever before having regard to the expansion of this industry which means so much to us not only in the maritimes and in Newfoundland but also to those who fish in inland waters, as mentioned by the minister this morning when he referred to the inland fisheries.
I am now going to come to what I think is an important branch of the development having regard to Nova Scotia. It will be recalled that prior to 1920 fish was distributed in only five forms: canned, salted, smoked, frozen whole and fresh. It was distributed to a large extent in bulk. Commencing at that time around 1920 distributors at the market purchased fish from dealers at the coast largely in the round form and processed it into fillets at the market. The processors at the coast gradually took over packaging and processing. At Halifax and other places we are concerned

Supply-Fisheries
with the development of the fresh and frozen fish industry of the Atlantic seaboard. While I know that figures are not easy to follow, I wish to mention a few to show the marked increases which have taken place since 1932. in that year Canada exported to the United States 671,100 pounds of fresh and frozen codfish. Please note that I said "fresh" and "frozen". There is no suggestion that fillets were frozen and exported in that year. Hence we can assume that the export fillet trade has developed since that time.
In 1946, fourteen years later, Canada exported 39,168,000 pounds of cod fillets. I could also refer to the 1,125,000 pounds of fresh and frozen haddock shipped in 1932 and the increased amount of 3,022,000 haddock fillets shipped in 1946. You will therefore see, Mr. Chairman, the great increase which took place during that fourteen years. This has been a remarkable increase.
The total quantity of cod fillets produced in Nova Scotia in 1932 was 1,760,670 pounds. In 1946-and these are the most recent figures I have-18,509,600 pounds were produced. Of haddock fillets, in 1932 there were produced 3,882,860 pounds; in 1946, 3,194,000 pounds. These figures forcefully indicate the trend of change in the industry. It will be noticed that there is little change in the volume of haddock, but codfish, once despised, has come into popular demand.
Meanwhile, other countries have more than kept pace with Canadian efforts, both in the increase in volume and in the development of other species, both of which factors have created intense competition for the Canadian producer. I am therefore suggesting that the entire face of the fishing industry has undergone a complete change, and the policies inaugurated around 1929 or just prior to 1932, still being in existence, probably do not meet current requirements.
I pause here, Mr. Chairman, again to compliment the minister on his expanded policy. From the policy inaugurated and announced this morning I believe we in the maritimes shall profit to a very great extent, and I particularly have Nova Scotia in mind.
It would appear that the major problem facing the fishing industry, or at least the operator, is the shortage of raw material, which problem arises out of the lack of modern production vehicles, as well as a diversion of edible sea foods to bait services. Lack of raw materials creates certain major problems in the conduct of production and merchandising. I think the minister is familiar with that problem, and I am going to suggest a few subheadings, which read as follows:	one, increasing overhead costs
become excessive when applied to the small 
volumes available; two, difficulty is found in recruiting, retaining and satisfying suitable plant personnel; three, because of the first two factors, irregular employment is created; and, four, plant personnel cannot become proficient in exercise of skill.
I want to ask a question. Has it now got to the point that hon. members must rise in their places and read essays on certain subjects? What is your view, Mr. Chairman?

When I have been speaking in the past the hon. member has risen and raised the same objection. I have listened to hon. gentlemen talk at random quite often. I am trying to be as specific as possible in placing before the Minister of Fisheries constructive criticism, and in doing so I naturally have to refer to notes.
The hon. member talks at random once in a while.

The next point I should like to emphasize is that lack of continuity of supply engenders inefficient plant organization. As a businessman the hon. member should appreciate the definite manner in which I am placing these suggestions before the committee.

Mr. Chairman-
The Depuiy Chairman: The rule is clear that speeches must not be read. I understand that the hon. member for Halifax is about to conclude his remarks, and is following his notes.
Mr. Chairman, I would not want you to think that I am going to conclude my remarks immediately. I definitely want to make some constructive suggestions to the minister.
Read on.

My fifth point is that markets are lost to foreign competitors and other food products because of shortages. If I were asked, Mr. Chairman, to name which of these factors were the most important I would perhaps say lack of continuity of supply and losses sustained to foreign competition. These are the two outstanding factors that we must contend with, and I am sure that the minister and his parliamentary assistant will take note of them. To these factors must be added the expense of maintaining a sales force and sustaining advertising campaigns with inadequate market coverage. The minister brought that out this morning in his statement when he referred to the need of advertising and making known the good quality of fish so that

it could be brought from the sea to the table in such a state that it would be well received by those at the table. That can be done only by proper marketing and by making known to the consuming public the benefits of eating more and more good fish.
I desire to point out that the growth and expansion which I have outlined have been accomplished with a minimum advertising effort and merchandising. It is claimed by certain operators that because of restrictions pertaining to the industry, arising largely through the opposition to modernization, we are not in a position to meet foreign competition, and unless a change of policy is forthcoming we shall lose the markets we now have. Again I say to the minister that he has recognized that fact and has made a change. Because of that change I believe we shall not have the difficulty we have had in the past with regard to modern foreign competition. I well recall not so many years ago, Mr. Chairman, the opposition to the introduction of steel boats. As far as I can ascertain this opposition no longer exists. At that time the inshore fishermen felt that they could not find outlets for -their production. Credit for the improved condition of the inshore fishermen, it is believed, is due to the government's action in assisting these fishermen in the diversion of their efforts and in more profitable operations. Perhaps I could mention in particular government assistance rendered the lobster fishermen toward the improvement in the transportation of their product, and assistance in improving methods of curing, packing and grading salt and pickled fish, and in making modern transportation available in the expansion of highway systems to isolated villages. I think that has been a great help in providing collection services in the different provinces. That has been brought about largely through co-operation with the provincial highway departments, which have made possible the extension of good roads into those isolated fishing villages; thus providing a means of transportation from the fishing villages to the centres where the fish is disposed of.
Then again opposition to modernization was found to be coming from the deep sea fishermen who desired to enhance their earning opportunities by seasonal operations in salt and fresh fishing. To a great extent improved markets have eliminated their concern in that regard. Today I think it can be said the opposition comes primarily from the shipbuilding industry which naturally wishes to sell its services to the fishing industry. I wish I had time to develop this thought. Perhaps I shall do so at some
Supply-Fisheries
future date. I say that because of the policy placed before us this morning by the minister. He said that he would permit certain types of ships to come from the United Kingdom and also from the United States. By that announcement he is going to meet the opposition to the competition which we have had to face in the maritimes in respect to a foreign type of ship which was permitted to fish off our banks at a time when we were unable to compete with that same type of ship. Because of that we were losing much wealth in our own country.
To regard this problem objectively, we must recognize that durability and efficiency of steel are essential to modern industry. I think the action taken by the minister will bring about the results desired, and we shall then be able to improve and operate along economic lines and thus compete with the modern foreign equipment. I feel, Mr. Chairman, that the steps taken this morning will be of real assistance to our fishing industry, and will also aid the shipbuilding activities of our country. As I understood the statement made this morning by the minister, it is to the effect that when one fishing concern brought a ship into this country, either from the United Kingdom or from the United States in particular, that firm would be obliged immediately to lay down a keel for a fishing vessel or a ship of a similar type. If they could not-
May I just make one correction? It is just the reverse. When they have laid down a keel in Canada then they may bring in a secondhand boat either from England or the United States.

Thank you. I will say that as soon as a company shows enterprise by laying down the keel for a new fishing ship, they are then at liberty to bring in one foreign ship of the type mentioned by the minister. I say that should add greatly to our position in the matter of meeting competition from foreign ships.
I should like also to draw the attention of the minister to the need of storage refrigeration facilities along the Atlantic coast, as well as in other sections of Canada. I do not believe the minister touched on this matter this morning. As of August 1, 1949, the very latest figures I was able to procure, cold storages on the Atlantic seaboard were congested with some 5,860,000 pounds of herring and 3,110,000 pounds of mackerel, a large proportion of which will be used in bait services. This was mentioned in a speech made recently by the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough (Mr. Kirk). He enlarged upon the matter to some extent, and I suggest his remarks should be kept in

Supply-Fisheries
mind by the minister, his parliamentary assistant and his officials when we are dealing with this matter of enlarged storage facilities.
Total holdings of frozen fish on the Atlantic seaboard as of August 1 were 19,070,000 pounds; hence, approximately 47 per cent of the total cost of storage constitutes a dead burden on the industry. This is an uneconomical method of conducting business. The industry now finds it necessary to use this fish as bait, and carry this burden of services. It is suggested that this burden could be converted to an asset by diverting this large volume of edible food into human food channels.
It is felt that this factor is a real argument in favour of modernization of fishing vessels, or the shipping to which I have referred. Reference was made earlier to the development of other species of fish for the human-food market. In particular it is desired to mention the rosefish industry developed in the United States, which commenced in 1934 when 539,000 pounds of fish were sold.
In the port of Gloucester alone in the year ending December 31, 1948, we find that 178,800,000 pounds of rosefish were landed at a value to the fishermen of $7,405,740. That is the point I had in mind a moment ago when I said there was much wealth being lost to Canada by not using modern fishing equipment.
Except to the extent that Newfoundland processors have recently produced redfish fillets, Canada has not participated in this development, even though 60 per cent of the raw material used in this development was taken off the shores of Nova Scotia. Contemplating the policies governing the expansion of the fishing industry on the Atlantic seaboard, it appears that the department, in view of the announcement this morning, has recognized the value of this type of fish. I am very pleased to note this expansion in policy and, as I said before, it is my view that if this is continued we will certainly add greatly to'the wealth of our fishing industry.
In closing I would say that the increased production of fish processors would have the effect of adding to the numbers employed. In his remarks the minister stated that they were not operating to capacity. One processor told me that he was operating at about 70 per cent of capacity. With the increased catch he would then be able to employ steadily a larger number of employees, and increase his production by 30 per cent, or bring it up to its 100 per cent capacity.
I say the policy the minister announced should add to employment as well as to the improvement of the fishing industry itself.

I would ask the minister to let the committee know what he and his department are doing in regard to oceanography. Two or three weeks ago I received a copy of the magazine Think in which appears an article entitled "Science of the Sea", and the article proceeds to show that the science of the sea is that of oceanography.
Because of this article I placed on the order paper certain questions to which I received full replies. I sent those replies to the fishing interests in Nova Scotia, who were pleased indeed to learn of the steps already taken to carry on studies in this important field of science, so far as the fishing industry is concerned. I hope the minister will be in a position later to enlarge upon the statement he made this morning by telling the committee what the department proposes to do. I am of the opinion that we should have greater study and training in connection with this subject, both on the extreme west and east coasts. At a meeting of Canadian universities last June this question was studied and a resolution was passed favouring the inauguration of studies on both coasts.
In closing I would ask the minister or his parliamentary assistant to comment on the following matters:
Will the increased use of steel fishing boats assist our fishing industry, and to what extent? I believe the answer can be given in the affirmative, but I should like to know the extent. I am referring to the minister's suggestion this morning concerning the use of a larger type of boat.
Will consideration be given to the production and processing of the rosefish so as to cater to additional markets?
Would the minister advise the committee as to what steps are being taken in respect to oceanography?

speakeroldname: Mr. G. F. Higgins (St. John's East):
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, it was a pleasure to listen to the minister this morning deliver an excellent speech in which he outlined the policy of his department. I have already offered to him my congratulations on other occasions; today he has shown the obvious interest he has in his work and the attention he has paid to his department since he assumed leadership of it.
The minister's statement was all-embracing, and indicated clearly the amount of work that has been done by him and by his staff. It was particularly encouraging to the fish-eries-minded persons from the new province. Hon. members may not realize it, but the fishing industry of Canada is a $200 million industry. As the Prime Minister said in September when addressing the fisheries council of Canada, a long time ago two fishes fed a large crowd; today the fishing industry

of Canada can indeed feed a large crowd if it is properly encouraged and if the proper care is taken of it, as the minister indicated today.
The minister made one statement this morning which rather made me sit up and wonder whether I understood it correctly. He referred to the new trawlers which it was proposed to build, and said that many foreign vessels were catching fish right up to our coastal limits. Advocating the building of new trawlers, he said that licences will be issued also to the better types of secondhand trawlers, bought either in the United States or in the United Kingdom, and registered in Canada after the payment of duty. To me that statement was a startling one, knowing, as I do, something about the fisheries on the Grand Banks. On a fine day there it looks like a gathering of the United Nations, because you see ships flying the flags of Portugal, Spain, Iceland, Norway, France, the United States and Canada. I think we all know what has happened to the United States fishing grounds. Through the use of trawlers they have been cleaned out, and now they are coming up to the Canadian grounds to fish.
Is the hon. member referring to the use of a trawler in the sense of a fishing schooner, or to the newer method of trawling or dragging?

I have no practical knowledge of the fishing industry, certainly nothing like the knowledge of the hon. member for Grand Falls-White Bay, but, as I understand it, trawling of any kind is dangerous to the future of our fishing industry. The minister will be able to deal with this much better than I, but I am told that by the use of trawlers many of the small fish are killed in the bringing up of the general haul. Because of the pressure, many of the small fish cannot get out and are killed.
The point I am trying to make is that the United States banks have been cleaned out and United States trawlers are now a dime a dozen. They now come down to the Grand Banks and the banks outside Halifax in order to fish. The use of trawlers may or may not be bad, but I think members such as the hon. member for Halifax should be worried about how our fishing industry will be affected. What is going to happen to our inshore fishing, the small man who works out from his home with his motorboat and dories? If trawlers are to fish right up to his front door, what is to become of him and his family? He will have no livelihood. I may be voicing the views of an amateur, but I submit that this is a serious matter for the industry. The little experience I have had would lead me to
Supply-Fisheries
believe that there is a real danger to the Canadian fisheries. We know what has happened to the European fisheries, and we know what has happened to the United States fisheries. Is it to happen to our fisheries as well?
I do not believe the minister will allow it to happen.
The same thing is happening to our seal fishing. During the past few years more foreign fishing boats have been fishing in Newfoundland waters. Last year some six or seven Norwegian seal fishers came to our waters. Some regulations will have to be prepared to cover this matter as well. After all, these fisheries are ours

and I speak in the national rather than the provincial sense. They offer great future possibilities, and they should not be destroyed.
As I say, consideration will have to be given to the effect of trawler operations upon the inshore fisheries of Canada. I shall not say anything more on this matter at the moment, because I am quite certain some of my colleagues from Newfoundland will wish to speak on this subject, and will be able to do so with more authority.
I was glad to hear the minister say that more would be done in the way of fish conservation. I was glad to hear that a kitchen has been set up in his department to demonstrate the proper cooking of fish. I understand that the per capita consumption of fish in Canada is ten pounds per year as compared with the European consumption of about forty-five to fifty pounds per year. If we can get the Canadian people to eat another five pounds per year, which is not very much to ask, I doubt if the fishing industry will be able to catch sufficient fish to meet the domestic demand.
When hon. members go home to their constituencies they should advocate the eating of fish. They should not forget that fish is a great brain food. From this point of view there may be hon. members who would not want to have their constituents eating too much fish; but it is worth thinking about.
On what does the hon. member base his assertion that fish is a brain food?

All I have to say is, look at the Newfoundland members.
The minister also referred to the salmon and lobster fisheries. In Newfoundland we are particularly interested in salmon fishing, which is extremely valuable. The British Columbia members, I assume, are also keenly interested in salmon fishing, but there is some difference between the Pacific and the Atlantic salmon. Pacific salmon

Supply-Fisheries
make their runs up the rivers once a year The minister also referred to the fisheries
and die, whereas the Atlantic salmon spawn a number of times.
The Atlantic salmon are being fished with cod nets much too close to the rivers. I have no doubt this is happening in the Nova Scotia rivers as well. I know definitely that our salmon catch is steadily dropping, and unless serious measures are taken to conserve our salmon fisheries in the not too distant years there is going to be a very poor outlook for salmon. I do not know whether this matter comes under the minister, or whether it is in the jurisdiction of the province, but I suggest that it might be advisable in certain of our rivers, where the fishermen now are catching the salmon as they enter, to take on those fishermen as wardens or something of the kind. In other words they might be paid the amount they would ordinarily obtain by fishing, and have these rivers kept free for the fish coming in.
Do I make my point clear? In each of these little bays where the rivers enter there tire probably ten or twelve fishermen catching salmon. They take large quantities of fish, for which they receive very low prices. If these people could be subsidized, by the amount of their average earnings over a two or three year period, and not put their nets in those rivers, I think it would be well worth while. The hon. member for Halifax is aware of the great salmon fisheries that existed in Nova Scotia in the early days, and he knows the conditions there now. You have to be a pretty smart fisherman to catch a fish in some of those rivers in the mari-times these days, and we do not want that to happen in Newfoundland. In all sincerity I offer that suggestion to the minister, from my experience as an amateur fisherman, as something which might well help solve the problem in our province.
The minister mentioned canned fish, and this brings to mind a very interesting development, of which no doubt the minister is aware. In the Financial Post of November 5 there was an article describing the shipping of live lobsters in tins. This is an unusual development and the article states:
The project was originated by J. E. MacDonald, a Boston seafoods packer, who has established an operation in Prince Edward Island, believed to be the first of its kind in the world.
If this is feasible, as apparently it is, we might create a market for lobsters in many parts of the world where they cannot be sold at the present time. As I say, the minister is probably aware of this development, and I merely mention it for the information of the committee.
prices support board. In Saturday Night of October 25 I saw this item in that connection:
The fisheries prices support board spent more than one million dollars buying a variety of fish to support prices, but managed to sell less than $12,000 worth. It marked off more than $500,000 as total loss and still has an inventory of about $634,000 worth of fish products at the end of the fish year, March 31, 1949.
I do not know whether that is correct, but if it is, I believe something should be done about it. It is all very well to support the industry; I agree with that in every way, but would it not be very much better to give those fish products to some of the countries that need food at the present time instead of holding them in stock? Otherwise they will go bad and be of no use to anyone. I think all hon. members will agree that when our warehouses are stocked with butter, fish and other commodities, as they are today, and when people in other parts of the world are hungry-
That is exactly what we did with the fish we bought; we gave it away to needy people.

Thank you; I did not know that. You may count on my active support in a program of that kind; I believe it is a splendid idea, and I think all hon. members will agree with it. I wonder if the Minister of Agriculture is going to give away his butter.
I thoroughly agree with the proposed packaging of fish and the general program envisaged by the minister in connection with fish inspection.
I have no comment to offer on the fine statement he made today, with which I entirely agree, except with respect to these trawlers; and on that note I should like to close my remarks. I believe serious difficulties may be avoided by proper precautions and proper protection with respect to trawlers. We have to think of the ordinary little man who is carrying on as a fisherman, and what is to become of him. If the hook-and-line man who depends upon his dory and his motorboat to get a few fish is to be put out of business by trawlers operating right on his doorstep, then I am afraid a great number of people may be on the dole in the not too distant future. It is something we must guard against. I should like to feel sure that we are not going to have any United Nations gathering out on our fishing banks, which I believe should be recognized as Canadian banks and preserved for Canadian fishermen.

The minister was kind enough to tell me he was going to answer a number of questions I submitted to him earlier. I do not know whether he would be prepared to give those answers now, but I believe he has the questions before him; therefore I need not repeat them. If he is prepared to answer them, I should be glad to get the information.
I did not wish to interrupt the hon. member, but would he be good enough to tell us when any inshore fishermen ever took his dory to the Grand Banks?
Not in a dory, of course; I did not say that.
That is what the hon. member implied.

I say the trawlers are going beyond the Grand Banks, and will soon be . fishing on the very doorsteps of these men. That is what is going to happen. I do not know whether the hon. member advocates the unlimited use of trawlers. He comes from the maritimes; surely he would not.
Is the hon. member aware that at the present time there are restrictions in regard to the distance within which trawlers may be used?

I see the hon. member for Grand Falls-White Bay in his place, and he would be much more competent to answer those questions than I am. All I know is that I am very much concerned about the use of trawlers, and I made that remark because I feel that definite restrictions will have to be imposed upon their use.
Apparently you do not know.

I come from a constituency that is outstanding for its fresh-water fishermen and fish. If the lake Superior trout is properly cooked, it will compare favourably with any other fish to be found anywhere.
I have sat in this house in past years and listened to the battles that were fought by members from the Pacific and Atlantic coasts for various reforms in connection with our fisheries, and now those reforms are being brought about. I am sure if the former hon. member for New Westminster were in the house now he would be happy to see so many of his suggestions put into effect.
I have a request to make of the minister.
I know at one time the department issued a cookbook showing how to cook fish. I wonder if the department has another, or if it has an improved edition of the original cookbook. My suggestion, which I think would help him carry out his policy, is that he send perhaps
Supply-Fisheries
a hundred of these recipe books to each member of the house and each member of the other place, so that they could put them in the envelopes with their Christmas greetings. It would not cost a great deal, and even if each hon. member had to contribute the cost I think it would be well worth while.
When I think of the minister and the way he speaks in the house, and when I consider the results he has achieved, I think of a man whose accomplishments speak louder than his words. We hope he may be long spared to continue to bring about these reforms.

I do not
agree with the remarks made by the hon. member for Queens when he says that when the fisheries department announced a policy, he would like to hear the minister say "I will do such a thing," instead of "I should". I believe the minister can say "I have done those things," because I believe much credit is due to him for the improvement that has taken place in the fishing industry in the last few years. It is my opinion that more has been done to promote the interests of the fishermen during the last fifteen years than was done in all the years previous to that.
Let me give you an instance. In my county, until a few years ago, deep-sea fishing was carried out in schooners valued at about $2,500. They were powered by a gasoline motor, and the method of fishing was by a hand line or set line. Through the assistance given by this government, today we have sixteen draggers each of which cost in the vicinity of from $25,000 to $30,000. Some of these boats have brought in over one million pounds of fish in the last season; that is a lot of fish, Mr. Chairman. The whole system of the fishing industry on the north shore of New Brunswick has been revolutionized.
I do not believe too much praise can be given the minister for the businesslike way in which he has tackled these problems, and the policies which he has inaugurated. By talking to the fisherman themselves, the shippers and the packers, he has created a better spirit. They appreciate that they must throw their efforts behind the program of the fishing industry. I believe that by bringing these people together, the minister has promoted a better spirit between the fishermen in the province and the buyers. I hope that the new policies the minister mentioned this morning will be adopted promptly, for I am sure they will mean a great expansion in the production of fish, especially in the maritime provinces. I believe the total production of fish in the

Supply-Fisheries
maritime provinces is approximately 100 million pounds. I can safely say that it would be easy to double this amount.
We are finding new markets for our fish. The trend today is towards fresh fish. In my county, most of the fish produced a few years ago was processed by the sun-cure method, and shipped to the European market. Today that same fish is being turned into fresh fillets, and is finding a ready market in the nation to the south of us. This has meant a much higher standard of living for the fisherman, for he is getting better prices than he was formerly. During the depression years, I recall fishermen selling dried codfish for as low as $3.50 or $3.75 a quintal which is about 112 pounds, and it took 220 pounds to make a quintal. Today, a fisherman is receiving 2\ cents for round fish, which means that these draggers I have mentioned produce about $25,000 worth of fish in a short season of five months. This means a great development for the fishing industry.
I may say that the fisherman has enjoyed a good season, and the fishing industry is the one thing in New Brunswick that has not shown any disturbing signs. In lumbering and other industries, there are signs of a recession, but the fishing industry has bright prospects. I hope that with assistance, such as was given by the government in the past, the fishermen will continue to prosper, for they have seen too many difficult years.

First, I should like to congratulate the minister on the statement he made today. I am convinced in my own mind that, some time in the near future, we may expect the fisheries department to become a major department instead of the minor department it has been since confederation. It would be impossible to place too much importance on the fishing industry in this country. Many people are dependent upon it for their livelihood and, with proper management, it could be greatly improved. The welfare of our fishermen could be improved, also.
This great improvement, which I expect to see some time in the future, can be brought about when the fishermen of this country are taught to produce a better article. I have stated repeatedly that the Department of Fisheries, instead of trying to educate the fisherman to produce a better article, regimented the fishermen too much. They were told what they must do, and they were never given any assistance. Today I believe the department is teaching young men in their employ to be of assistance to the IMr. Richard (Gloucester).]
fishermen. When you find the employees of the fisheries department making friends with the fishermen, advising them, and helping them with their problems, you will find the industry will improve.
Speaking of the loss of markets in Canada, I believe that the fish-canning industry of this country has been hit harder than any other industry from the Atlantic ocean to the Pacific. Very little is said about it, however. During the war no trouble was experienced in marketing anything that could be put into a can. I often wondered why, when shipping space was so valuable, Britain could take any quantity of canned fish we were able to produce. In many cases, that fish was a gift from this country to Britain. When the war was over, after the fishing industry had gone a long way in assisting that country, we found they had no more use for Canadian fish.
Some people will say that the British have not the exchange. A little over a year ago I was in Britain and I was disturbed on being informed that Russian salmon was appearing on the British market. It was not bought with sterling, but the British had bartered tin plate for this Russian salmon. At that time all the warehouses in British Columbia were filled with salmon. I know that many of the delegates who were there tried to buy the B.C. salmon to take back to their country, not just a few cases, but carloads. They had to take this Russian salmon. It has not been explained to me why the tin plate could not have been bartered for Canadian fish.
The statement made by the Minister of Agriculture which was quoted in today's press is in line with what I have thought since the war ended in 1945. I do not believe Britain has treated this country the way it should have been treated; that is my personal opinion, but I do not hesitate in expressing it. We did everything we could to help Britain. We made gifts and loans of over $5 billion, yet today when we want to sell fish or anything that is produced in this country, the British turn it down. No reasonable explanation has been given to me for this state of affairs.
Previous to the war, the little county from which I come was shipping canned fish to one hundred different countries in the world, many of them within the commonwealth. Today this market has been lost to a great extent. In former years, we had no trouble disposing of all we had to offer. The quality is the same today or better, but it is utterly impossible to get into that British market and sell anything we produce down in the maritime provinces.

From following the discussions I have learned that one should not refer to previous debates in the house, but we have heard it said, and we have been warned, that we should watch carefully our neighbours down to the south of us. For just a few minutes I want to tell hon. members what those neighbours down to the south of us mean to the people of the maritime provinces. We will take the lobster industry, for instance, which is a big industry in the maritime provinces. In the four maritime provinces and the state of Maine we produce practically all the lobster that are produced on the North American continent.
What is that?
I said that in the maritime provinces and in the state of Maine we produce practically all the lobsters that are produced on the North American continent.
I thought you said on the North American continent.

That is what I said, on the North American continent, and I think that statement is correct. More than 95 per cent of those lobsters produced in the maritime provinces are sold in the United States. Those figures are correct. About 60 per cent of the sardines that are caught in the section of the country in which I live are sold in the United States. Ninety per cent of the scallops dragged in the bay of Fundy are sold in the United States. About 80 per cent of the groundfish caught in that section of the country are sold in the United States. We have another industry that few people know anything about. That is the herring scale industry. It may sound trivial to hon. members but the herring scale industry in my part of the country means hundreds of thousands of dollars to the fishermen. They are sold 100 per cent in the United States of America.
When we speak of the balance of trade, I often wonder if the people of Ontario and Quebec realize just exactly the position we are in down in the maritimes. There is nothing that we have to offer that they want in central Canada. We are obliged to go to our neighbours to the south of us in order to sell our products. But when we bring that money back into Canada, if there is anything that we might want for our homes we have to go to Ontario and pay two prices for it. Those are actual facts. There is nothing they want to buy from us but they are always ready to sell.
I have told this story on many occasions. Down where I live there are many hundred of articles that I can buy in the United
Supply-Fisheries
States for fifty per cent of what is charged for them in Canada. That is no exaggeration. 1 can give you the price tag if you want it.
Give us some.
Very well. I saw a refrigerator in Calais, Maine, one month ago for $165.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order. I would ask the hon. member to confine his remarks to the item under discussion.

If the hon. member wants a reply, he is welcome to it. The same article sells for $340 in Canada, made by the same company.
When you speak of balance of trade I wonder why we down there are obliged to find markets somewhere else, but when it comes time to buy something we need for our own homes-and these are not luxuries today, we would all like to get them for our homes-we have to come up here and pay the people in Ontario two prices for them. I might mention here the austerity program that was put into effect a short time ago and which to my mind was necessary at that time. The manufacturers of this province took full advantage of it, and when the. time comes for all restrictions to be removed, you will see the price of the article I have mentioned decrease 33 per cent overnight. They are taking full advantage of conditions.
To show you that these people to the south of us, who many of our friends think are selfish, are not as selfish as they might be, 1 want to read a very short piece from the Maine Coast Fisherman, which in my estimation is one of the best fishing magazines published anywhere on the North American continent. The editorial is headed "Lobster Tariff" and it reads as follows:
"Why don't they put a tariff on Canadian lobsters?" lobstermen frequently ask. It doesn't look to us as though there is much chance of such a tariff ever being put into effect.
Our government, expressing the will of the majority, has adopted a free trade policy. We Americans have told the world we believe in lower tariffs everywhere to encourage greater interchange of goods. We believe the trade thus created leads to better economic conditions. We believe this helps world peace.
Even if a tariff were set up, it is questionable whether it would help the Maine lobsterman in the long run.
This is the state of Maine. To continue:
It is an artificial way of forcing the consumer to pay a higher price for lobster. Furthermore, Maine cannot possibly supply the whole market. There would be fewer people eating lobster and paying a good deal more for it. The market would contract, the consumer would rebel, and sooner or later we'd be worse off than we were before.

Supply-Fisheries
That is the attitude of the Fisherman in the state of Maine, with whom we are competing today. That magazine is read by every fisherman in the state of Maine and that is the opinion expressed by the editor. If they should put a prohibitive tariff on fish that are caught in the maritime provinces, you could buy the maritime provinces for $1.50 an acre and you would take a big loss. We are wholly dependent on that market.
I am not going into the confederation issue. But many times, when people tell me that I am an American, I wonder whether, if at the time of confederation we in the maritime provinces had decided that we should like to go on the other side of the border, we would not be better off today. Again, as I say, I never hesitate in expressing my personal opinion; and that is my opinion at the present time. Under the set-up in this country I believe that if we were part of the United States there would be a great deal more prosperity in the maritime provinces than we are enjoying at the present time. There is nothing that we can sell in central Canada. The only thing we can do is to buy there and to pay two prices for what we buy.
I intended to be brief when I rose to my feet, and I think I shall stick to that idea. If we wish to help the fishing industry, it can be done with quality only. The one thing that will assist the industry is to produce better quality. I know the minister has that in mind, and I believe the department is behind him 100 per cent. You might market fish products marked "C.S." Canada standard, but that is not going to sell it. It is the quality that is in the can that is going to sell it. To a great extent I believe the trade mark is the thing that catches the eye of the purchaser. In order to produce better quality an educational program must be encouraged by the fisheries department. I have this statement to make before I sit down. Rather than go out among the fishermen and tell them that they cannot do this, that they cannot do that, hale them into court, fine them and do everything you can to make it disagreeable for them to get along, if the members of the fisheries department forget all about that idea and consider the fishermen their friends and act as their advisers, the fishing industry can go a long way.

had not intended to say much at this time, Mr. Chairman, but the minister's statement this morning has aroused my interest in this discussion. It was without doubt a most comprehensive statement of government policy. It was the most comprehensive one I have ever heard of government policy with regard to the fisheries in this country; and I

am firmly convinced that it is the beginning of a big national plan in the great fishing industry.
I do not want to keep the house too long and I shall therefore be as brief as I can. I might ask the indulgence of hon. members, bearing in mind the fact that I have occupied so little of the time of the house up until this time; if I should delay them for five minutes or so I hope I shall not lose any friends.
I do not want to spend any time talking about quality. That is something that was discussed at great length in the house some time ago. The department and everyone else in the country is now well aware that the success of the fishing industry depends to a large extent on the quality of the product.
I was glad to note in the statement made by the minister this morning that some emphasis is to be put on the establishment of consumer services. That is an excellent idea. In that regard I have just one thing to say, namely, that it does appear to me, and to many others in the east at least, that when the fishery cookbooks were sent to the publisher they came off the presses with complicated recipes for the preparation of fish. They contained substances to put into the cooking of fish which were hard to obtain. I should like to emphasize that the more simply fish is cooked the better it is. There are three or four changes that are most important. The fish must be bought in fresh condition. It may be cooked simply or otherwise but it must be cooked quickly, and certainly it must not be cooked too much. The fourth part of the change so far as the consumer is concerned is that as soon as it is cooked it must be served. Many of us from the maritimes have noticed that in the best hotels and the best restaurants of this country it is most difficult to get fish such as we would have served every day, if we like it that often, in our own homes.
I also regret to say that even in the best hotels and the best restaurants in Nova Scotia they have not yet arrived at a point where they can serve fish of a quality equal to that served in most of the homes along the fishing shore of the province.
I want to say just a word about the institution of technical services. The objectives outlined in the statement made by the minister were certainly sound, and I was glad to note that the department realized the necessity of able and qualified personnel in regard to the advisory services of a technical nature. In this regard I think it will be generally realized that qualified personnel is not easily available. 1 hope that the department will recognize that this kind of service will not

oe helpful to the fishermen and to the fish processors unless it is staffed by qualified personnel. In my dealings with the Department of Fisheries I have found that they are always open to suggestions. I would hope that they would be open to the varied suggestions that are made in this discussion today.
The second point in the statement made by the minister, apart from quality, was the reference to the quantity. That reference to quantity concerned itself with something about trawlers. Some years ago on certain parts of the east coast there was quite a lot of opposition to the establishment of trawlers to any great number. There was a movement on foot which would have resulted in the banning of all licences for trawlers; but I do not think that the fishermen and those concerned with the fishing industry are as prejudiced today as they were some years ago. I think it is realized by all that there is need for trawler fish to ensure continuity of supply, even though a great deal of the trawler fish is very inferior in quality to that which is obtained by fishing from small boats. I am not quite clear on the reasons for the proposed encouragement of the operation of more trawlers. Is it that present market demands are not being met by the present methods of fishing? If that is so I think all progress should be made in modernizing fishing methods to secure all the fish that can be sold. But if market demands at the present time are met I should think that restricted action with regard to the issuing of licences for trawlers would be advisable. It would be advisable until the expansion of the market has demonstrated the absolute necessity of going into the larger productive method. I am quite sure that the farmer would not expand his farm without some knowledge of the future market. I do not think that many manufacturers would increase the capacity of their plants unless they were fairly certain that there was a market that they could supply at a profit. If this market does not exist at the present time, or if the market which we now have shrinks-that is a factor which is feared by a great many people in the fish business-
I am wondering what the effect of more licences will be on these small boat owners of our province. In the constituency which I have the honour to represent there are actually thousands of those small boats, and these people are really the backbone of our economy. They are the backbone of our national effort in peace or in war, as has been very well demonstrated in the past.
I should like to point out that these small boats are getting larger. I do not mean they are getting soaked in the water, but the
2787
Supply-Fisheries fishermen are gradually moving from smaller sized boats to larger sized boats. There was a time not very many years ago when fishing from so-called small boats was done close to the shore; but now there is a large number of these boats of a size which permits them to go quite a number of miles out to sea to fish on the banks. They go on two-day trips or longer. They are going to be worried, and I am going to be worried about the economy down there in connection with the questionable injury and the possible destruction of those grounds which are reached by these medium-sized boats. The western Nova Scotia fishermen will have great fears of the effect of any large increase in trawler licences. I have no doubt that the department is also aware of all these angles and will not grant licences to the detriment of the small-boat fishermen.

speakeroldname: Mr. W. J. Browne (Si. John's West):
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, although I did not have the pleasure of hearing the minister's speech this morning I have had the opportunity of reading it since. I would like to congratulate him on the manner in which he delivered his speech. I am sure he has taken a great interest m the fisheries of the maritimes, of Newfoundland and of the west coast as well. Since Newfoundland is very much concerned with fisheries I feel I would be recreant in my duty today if I did not make some observations on some of the statements which are to be found in the minister's speech.
The fisheries of Newfoundland are the most important industry in that province. Although the value of pulp and paper may exceed the gross value of the fisheries, nevertheless in the distribution of the returns the fisheries take first place. The fisheries concern more people. There are 30,000 fishermen, and they are scattered all over the island, all around its six thousand miles of coast line. Observations have been made in regard to the trawlers. As everyone knows, trawlers are boats that carry around twenty or thirty men. I know how they operate out of St. John's. When they were introduced into St. John's just a few years ago these boats operated in this way. They would come in with a load of 200,000, 250,000 or 300,000 pounds of fish, unload them and off they would go again, once a week, regularly just like a train on a schedule. I know the people who have brought these trawlers in and financed them are doing very good work. They have two or three very modern plants in St. John's. A number of people are employed at these plants when the fish come in, but I do not think, Mr. Chairman, that that fishery is to be compared with the salt, cod fishery-that is, with the fishery that the people engage in around the Newfoundland!
27S8

Supply-Fisheries
coast. Take any of the little settlements around Newfoundland where the men are engaged in hook-and-line fishing or in trawling or in trapping, and in curing their fish. Such fishing is important to the fisherman because it is his vocation, his livelihood. He does not have to leave his home and go to St. John's, living away from his family. It is a way of living for him. It is a better thing economically for our country than an intensification of fishing through the use of trawlers.
The minister said, in effect, that the department is reversing the policy of former years by giving more licences. What is the limit of the number of trawlers going to be? How many are going to engage in this enterprise?
At the present time we have the French, who are supposed to have forty new trawlers this year. We have the Spanish, and we have the Portuguese. I think the Portuguese are the best of them, because they fish from small boats. But these big draggers which go over the banks are doing the simplest kind of thing; they put out a big dragnet astern and steam across the banks. Then they turn around and go back, raking up everything from halibut to flounders and dogfish-they get everything in their nets. What they do not want they throw away. Many small fish are thrown away, and in that respect it is uneconomical.
We have all those different nationalities fishing out there, presenting a serious international problem, I would say. The minister spoke somewhat disparagingly about the backward areas. I believe he included in that statement areas in Newfoundland. Then he referred to the traditional markets in Europe and in the West Indies for Newfoundland and other maritime provinces in connection with the marketing of cod. What are we going to do with our traditional markets? Portugal and Spain have been buying and catching Newfoundland fish for over four hundred years.
I should like to correct that statement. Spain has hot bought any fish from Newfoundland for some years.

Well, if Spain has not bought any fish for some years, the fact is that Spain throughout the centuries has bought millions of quintals from us, and that country has been one of our principal markets. There may be a reason for the present condition, but it would not be in order to enter into a discussion of that today.
Portugal is the chief consumer of codfish, and salt cod is their principal article of diet. We do not need to give any lessons in cooking to the Portuguese, or any encouragement to
[Mr. Browne (St. John's West).)
the consumer in Portugal to have him eat our codfish. Why, therefore, should we speak disparagingly about them? But what do we buy from Portugal? It has been a matter of great regret that we have not been buying enough from Portugal, or from Spain or Italy or Greece or any of those countries which in the past have bought large quantities of our fish. We have not bought anything in comparison with the value of the fish they have bought from us. It is true that from the West Indies we do take molasses and some rum. But the value of the fish we export to the West Indies is greater than the value of the goods we buy in return.
My understanding is that at the present time we have a favourable balance of trade with both Spain and Portugal. In other words, we buy more from them than they buy from us.
The minister means that Canada as a whole is doing that?
Yes. And another thing: Portugal is now getting sixty per cent of her own requirements.

Of her own
requirements?
Yes.

The Portuguese, Spaniards and French have been catching fish on the banks for hundreds of years, just the same as the British, the Newfoundlanders and the Canadians.
In regard to the marketing of fresh fish, let me say that the commission of government in Newfoundland tried to develop this industry within the last few years. They encouraged the marketing of fresh fish to a great extent. They advanced hundreds of thousands of dollars in modern plant equipment to merchants who bought fresh fish from the fishermen. But, sir, is it not dangerous, as the hon. member for Charlotte has said, when by a stroke of the pen the government of the United States could put an embargo on fish so that all that business would be wrecked? Therefore we should not pay too much attention to the fresh fish market to the detriment or neglect of the salt fish market. What we want is to try to have a proper balance.
I am certainly glad to learn that the minister is going to establish an extensive technical service. We have had technical research at various periods throughout the last seventy or eighty years in Newfoundland. From time to time the Newfoundland government has experienced a wave of that sort of thing. During the past ten or twelve years, under the commission of government, in

accordance with the recommendations of the Amulree report the government carried out certain investigations along scientific lines. I believe that policy could be expanded.
There is one thing that can be beneficial to the fishermen-and the fishermen are the backbone of this industry. We must consider the fishermen in the first instance-and I am referring to the fishermen around the coast. What is their problem? It seems to me that the first problem of the fishermen is the purchase of supplies. I believe the provincial government is going to remedy that, because it has set up a new department of fisheries and co-operatives. They are not leaving everything to the federal government. The provincial government is going to do its share to assist in the promotion of the welfare of the fishermen. The co-operatives are going to encourage the co-operative purchasing of supplies, and this procedure will be helpful. The next question which arises in connection with fishing is the matter of bait. When the fishery is going well the two things that worry many fishermen are, first, a shortage of salt, and, second, a shortage of bait. Of these two the shortage of bait is the more serious as it is more frequent.
I have had correspondence with the minister in connection with the erection of bait depots, and I have suggested to him, as I now suggest to the committee, the advisability and feasibility of research being carried on with a view to setting up small bait depots instead of having large ones at central points. While those points may be accessible, still it would be more advantageous to the fisherman if he could have smaller bait depots in as many of the villages as possible. The fisherman will get up at two or three o'clock in the morning, and it is difficult for him to go, either by motorcar or by boat, back to" a bait depot fifteen or twenty miles away to get his bait, and then come back and go out fishing again. In fact it is impossible for him to do that and operate successfully. If there were smaller bait depots in the settlements it would become a comparatively simple matter for him to get his bait supplies.
There are three principal methods used by Newfoundlanders in the catching of codfish. One is by traps-and I do not think the minister could do much about that. Another is by trawl line-that is where the bait comes in; and another is by jigging. Then we have the big banker. These banking vessels operate off the south coast ports of Newfoundland with dories. The men go off in the dories to fish on the fishing banks with trawls, and catch the fish in that way.
As the minister knows, the complaint is sometimes made that the great draggers interfere with the work being done by the banking
Supply-Fisheries
vessels. I was glad to learn that the minister favours an interprovincial conference with the representatives of the federal government. I believe these problems should be considered at that time, particularly the matter of the establishment of bait freezers, and the undesirability of giving too many licences to trawlers. Too many of these trawlers would be bad for the economy of our country, particularly those sections of it in the maritime provinces and Newfoundland from which they would be operating.

Mr. Chairman, I shall speak briefly, because no one has spoken today from the west. I believe someone from the west coast should speak on these estimates. We are proud of the minister who comes from our province. This is one example where a businessman is doing a good job. With an industry controlling the large amount of money represented by the fishermen on the east and west coasts, we believe it is highly satisfactory to have a businessman at the head of the department, and that he is likely to do a more satisfactory job than could be done by a theorist. I think we all recognize that the minister has done a wonderful job in running his department. I think his accomplishments have been marvellous for a comparatively new minister.
The fishing industry which I represent on the west coast is happy over the progress that has been made. Some years ago they had not a great deal of confidence in the department. There are in my constituency some 2,000 fishermen who are centred around one of the largest canning factories in the world. These men now leave for the fishing grounds with the feeling that they are being looked after by the department. I go along with the hon. member for Newfoundland in saying that if the minister and the department are given time they will solve the difficulties of the industry in that province.

Mr. Chairman, there is a large fishing industry in the riding I represent and therefore I am interested in the minister's statement. This is the first time since I came to this house that a Minister of Fisheries has made a statement similar to the one we had today. This would seem to indicate that the department is taking hold of the industry in a realistic way. The minister has announced a program. Whether we agree with it in its entirety or not, the fact remains that there is a program. I am sorry that that program is not to be started until the estimates of next year provide the necessary finances. We should be doing something right away about the matters discussed by the minister in his statement.

Supply-Fisheries
The minister has said that he has two things in mind. First, there is the development of a market. That is necessary because there is not much use catching fish unless you can sell them. He tells us about the experimental kitchen that has been set up, and that is a good thing. The trouble with getting a larger consumption of fish in the past has been the fact that in many cases it was poorly prepared. Then the next thing is getting the fish from the source of supply to the market of consumption, and the minister indicates that steps are being taken along these lines.
I notice that some $80,000 is being provided in the estimates for co-operative education. For a long time I have been convinced that the only way to properly rehabilitate this industry is along these lines. You must get the people interested in the industry working on their own problems and accepting some responsibility, not only in connection with production and processing but in marketing as well. You cannot expect to make much progress working only from Ottawa or through some large fish company which is interested only in profits. There must be organization of those engaged in the industry on a co-operative basis. Ever since I have been a member I have noticed that from year to year, particularly in the minister's department, increasing amounts have been made available for co-operative work. The amount provided in the estimates this year is substantial and, as I say, that is the only way this industry can be made to work.
I should like to say a few words about the trawlers. I have gone to meetings of fishermen and have been in their halls when they have discussed this trawler question. As the senior member for Halifax indicated, foreign trawlers are not allowed to come closer than three miles and as such they do not affect the shore fishermen very much. The minister has indicated that licences are going to be granted to Canadian trawlers and to secondhand trawlers that have been built in the United Kingdom or the United States providing the company purchasing them lays down a new keel in Canada. I assume that is to stimulate shipbuilding, but it does not alter the fact that the shore fisherman takes a serious view of the trawler.
In my view the trawler is simply the mechanization of the industry. It is another technological advance that has to be reckoned with and if one is thinking ahead he cannot oppose it very well. The man with the small boat who must ggt up at four o'clock in the morning to go out and fish to earn an income of about $300 per year may lose his job, but he will not be losing very much.

The serious part of the trawler operation is the concentration of production. At the present time in Nova Scotia the whole industry is controlled by one company, the National Fish Company. The trawlers are going to fish for that company. That company also has a concentration of bait freezing and storage facilities at the different places along the shore. The shore fisherman will be placed in the position where he will have to work for that company on that company's terms; he will have to sell his fish to that company for whatever they want to pay. That is an angle the federal and provincial governments will have to consider. The shore fisherman is going to lose a not very good job through this process but will likely obtain a means of livelihood of some kind.
Another angle of the trawler question that is discussed by the fishermen with some heat is the charge that the trawler destroys the fishing grounds. I have heard this charged right along the whole coast of Nova Scotia. As the hon. member for St. John's West has said, a trawler will go out, put down its drag and then pull up anything that happens to come in contact with the drag. It keeps only a certain type of fish and perhaps fifty per cent of what is brought up by the drag is thrown back. After this goes on for some time there may be two or three feet of dead fish on the bottom and the live fish simply will not come in and feed. The result is a backing up of the fishing grounds. The shore fisherman cannot go out too far and in a few years' time there may be a complete destruction of the fishing grounds because of this practice.
I do not claim that I know all about this matter but I have heard men who make their living at fishing state that this is the case. In carrying out his new program the minister will have to give some regard to this claim. The perpetuation of the industry is something that should be guaranteed if at all possible.
I think the hon. member for St. John's West put his finger on a vital point when he referred to the bait freezing plants. I do not think it is an answer to the problem to concentrate the bait-freezing facilities at one or two points on the east coast. All along the coast are communities which have been built up around certain fishing grounds and I submit that a decentralization of the bait freezing facilities is necessary. I believe we should have smaller plants scattered along the shore and made available to the shore fishermen. I think that step is absolutely necessary; and I believe this also applies to storage facilities. You generally find the plant that has the bait also has the storage facilities, and unless you get the bait on that

company's terms you do not fish. Then when you come in with a load of fish, unless you sell it to that company on its own terms there is no space for your fish, so you throw them back into the water. Fishermen have told me that has actually happened. They brought in a catch; there was no storage space, so they threw the fish back.
The minister has made a survey, and he knows the situation. He has competent men in his department; I believe his deputy minister is one of the best men on the continent in that field. I have known of his work for a long time, and I believe he has the confidence of the people who fish. I hope he will just keep in mind that possibility of making bait and storage facilities available along the coast, instead of being concentrated at one point.
That is all I have to say, but I do want to compliment the minister on what he has done. This is the first time I have seen a Minister of Fisheries bring in his estimates and indicate to the house that he has surveyed the industry and drawn up plans for the future. I believe he is making a realistic approach to the whole problem, and I only hope he remains in the department until he has been able to complete this program.

want to bring just one matter to the attention of the minister, concerning which there has been a great deal of correspondence and as to which I have had a great many complaints. I feel that it should be brought directly to the attention of the minister so he may answer the question in the house, and in that way the people in the area to which I am going to refer will learn just what is going on.
I refer to the area off the county of Digby in the bay of Fundy. My understanding of the situation is that under our regulations Canadian draggers are permitted to operate up to within twelve miles of the coast, but that under international regulations United States draggers are permitted to operate up to within three miles of the coast. In addition we are continually receiving complaints to the effect that United States draggers are operating even within the three-mile limit. In this connection I have had a great deal of correspondence and many interviews with various officials of the department. I have found them most co-operative; they have sent in their patrol boats, but still the complaints come in that at night, after the patrol boats leave the grounds, these United States draggers operate within the three-mile limit.
With that brief background I want to ask the minister, when he replies to the various questions that have been asked, to explain
Supply-Fisheries
to hon. members and those engaged in fishing in that area what steps have been taken or are being taken or are proposed to be taken to rectify this situation. Here we are endeavouring to protect the fishing grounds by keeping our own draggers away, yet at the same time United States draggers are alleged to operate within three miles of the shore.

In reply to the hon. member who has just resumed his seat, only ten days ago we had a new boat come off the ways at Shelburne. That boat is either in that area now or will be there within a day or two. Last year and again this year we had complaints that United States boats were coming within the three-mile limit, but this new boat is in there now, and another, the Cygnus, the largest in our fleet, will be able to go around there again in about a week.
Before I answer the other questions which have been put to me I should like the privilege of placing on Hansard the answers to a number of questions asked a few days ago by the hon. member for St. John's East. I could read them, but that would take some time and with the permission of the committee I would place them on Hansard.
