speechtext: Is that the pleasure of the committee?
Agreed.

The questions and answers are as follows:
Statements on questions raised by the Newfoundland delegation during the negotiations for the union of Newfoundland with Canada:
1.	Trawling.
"Newfoundland trawlers will be permitted to fish (as they have been doing) to the three-mile limit off the coasts of Newfoundland, and an amendment to the Fisheries Act, 1932, will be introduced for this purpose.
It is understood that the policy as to trawlei licensing in Newfoundland will be based on securing the maximum efficiency for the province's fishing industry and welfare for its shore communities.
With respect to the establishment of territorial waters it is our understanding that the 'headland to headland' rule, as it now applies to Newfoundland, will continue to apply."
Comment:
An amendment to the Fisheries Act, 1932, has been passed which will permit Newfoundland trawlers to fish to the three-mile limit off the coasts of Newfoundland when the act is proclaimed in Newfoundland.
2.	Prohibition of export of bait fishes.
"At present the Customs and Fisheries Protection Act prohibits the sale of bait to foreign fishing vessels in Canadian territorial waters, except by special treaty or convention. An amendment to this act will be introduced in order to continue the practice now followed by Newfoundland in this matter."

Supply-Fisheries
Comment:
An amendment to the Customs and Fisheries Protection Act has been passed by the federal parliament which will permit this practice under the act when it is proclaimed in Newfoundland. Consultations have already been initiated with the province with a view to bringing this act in force.
3.	Licensing of premises to pack fish (including
filleting and freezing plants).
"It is understood that, while these matters will come under federal jurisdiction at the date of union, the Newfoundland fisheries board, during the time that it continues to operate, will be the medium through which application for licences will be made and the relevant regulations brought into effect." Comment:
The Newfoundland fisheries board continues to be the medium through which application for licences are made and the relative regulations brought into effect.
4.	Power of Newfoundland fisheries board to set
quotas for fish for export.
"This power, which is involved in the marketing operations of the Newfoundland fisheries board, will be retained as a marketing function during the life of the board."
Comment:
"This power, which is involved in the marketing function of the Newfoundland fisheries board.
5.	Market representatives.
" (a) The fish trade representatives of the Newfoundland fisheries board abroad (for which six positions exist and of which five are filled at present) will be continued as board officials, and be paid out of funds voted for the board during such time as the board remains in operation.
(b) The Department of Trade and Commerce will absorb into the Canadian trade commissioner service the two trade commissioners in London and New York, at present responsible to the Newfoundland department of natural resources."
Comment:
(a)	Trade representatives of the Newfoundland fisheries board are being continued as board officials. Six positions exist, of which four are filled at the present time, i.e., Jamaica, Puerto Rico, Portugal and Italy. Consideration is being given to the appointments of representatives to Brazil and one other market, possibly Cuba.
(b)	The Department of Trade and Commerce have absorbed into the Canadian trade commissioner service the two Newfoundland trade commissioners, who were stationed in London and New York.
6.	Newfoundland fish export tax.
"The export tax of five cents per quintal on the volume of fish exported from Newfoundland will be abolished at the date of union."
Comment:
This export tax no longer applies and was abolished at the date of union.
7.	Power of Newfoundland fisheries board to negotiate contracts.
"The Newfoundland fisheries board will not be required to deal through the Canadian Commercial Corporation, and may in its discretion continue to charge a fee or commission for its services in negotiating contracts, subject only to such export and import controls as may exist."
Comment:
The Newfoundland fisheries board is not required to deal through the Canadian Commercial Corporation in negotiating contracts and may continue to

charge a fee or commission for its services in negotiating contracts. The revised fish inspection bill will not affect this arrangement.
8.	Fish wrappers and packages.
"Wrappers provided by purchasers in the United States for their suppliers in Newfoundland will be dutiable after the date of union but will also be eligible for the ninety-nine per cent drawback on re-export as containers of fresh frozen fish.
Efforts are being made to arrange for the continued use for export of the present stock of wrappers marked 'Product of Newfoundland.'
Importation of printed wrappers of all kinds made from paper for domestic use is prohibited at the present time but permits may be granted by the Department of Finance in cases where the United States importer insists on supplying his own wrapper for the goods purchased by him in Canada. There is no restriction, however, on the importation of transparent wrappers or types of cardboard cartons or boxes usually used in the fish trade. These wrappers and containers are also eligible for the ninety-nine per cent drawback on re-export as containers of fresh frozen fish."
Comment:
Wrappers provided by purchasers in the United States for their suppliers in Newfoundland became dutiable after the date of union but at the same time became eligible for the ninety-nine per cent drawback on re-export as containers of fresh frozen fish.
Arrangements were made with the United States authorities for the continued use for export from Newfoundland of wrappers marked "Product of Newfoundland." The arrangement covered wrappers so marked as were on hand in Newfoundland at date of union.
9.	Inspection fees on export.
"The present policy is to make no charge for inspection services."
Comment:
No charge for inspection services has been made by the Newfoundland fisheries board since date of union. This is in line with policy covering the inspection of fish and fishery products throughout the rest of Canada.
10.	Tariff agreements.
"The position after union of the agreement between Newfoundland and the Dominican republic providing for a low rate of duty on imports of Newfoundland codfish into the latter country is being examined. If necessary the Canadian government will initiate discussions on this matter." Comment:
Under the Annecy trade negotiations of 1949 the Dominican republic kept dry salted codfish under the existing M.F.N. rate, thereby ensuring the continuation of the preferential rates originally established under the Newfoundland-Dominican agreement of 1940.
11.	Bait service.
"The Canadian government will seek legislation or take such other steps as may be necessary to provide that the Newfoundland bait service will be taken over and operated without fundamental change by the Department of Fisheries. If, after the date of union, changes are made for the benefit of Canada as a whole, the question of payment will be discussed between federal and provincial authorities."
Comment:
Since union the Newfoundland bait service has been operated by the Department of Fisheries without fundamental change.
Has the minister tabled the answers to all the questions, or has he an answer to my suggestion with respect to the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act?

The Minister of Agriculture, of course, is the authority on the P.F.R.A., but I think I am correct in saying that it is a program that was worked out to meet the effects of drought in the low rainfall areas of Saskatchewan and Alberta. The construction of dams, development of community pastures, introduction of new tillage methods, and so on, are all constructive solutions to the problems of the area.
The program I have just presented to this house outlines, I think, a constructive answer to the basic problems of the underdeveloped fishing areas of the Atlantic coast, including Newfoundland. The details of the fisheries program will be very different from the details of the P.F.R.A., of course, but the objectives will be somewhat the same. I have indicated that we propose to establish a technical service to provide fishermen, small plants and the wholesale and retail trade with technical help on the improvement of their individual operations. We propose to discover what are the best methods of fishing in the different areas and to carry out demonstrations for the benefit of the fishermen. What we have in mind is a constructive long-term solution for the low income areas where the resources and manpower are available, but where new methods of catching and processing fish are necessary to meet the demands of the modern world.
I do not wish to enter into any argument with respect to the trawler situation, but most certainly we would not have advocated a change of policy if there had not been a demand for more fish. Most processors, particularly in Nova Scotia, have not been able to supply that demand; in fact one community appears to be quite wrought up over the fact that we have been delayed so long in getting a boat to them. I am satisfied that in the over-all picture there will be more employment and that the standard of living of the fishermen and those on shore will be improved under this plan.
I want to leave just three thoughts with hon. members. At the present time in the maritime provinces we have the advantage of being closer to the grounds than the Americans; but the only way we can retain that advantage is by having equally good equipment, boats of the same speed and adequate gear. If we do not keep up our standard of boats and gear we will lose the advantage we have at the present time, and also lose the fish. The hon. member for St. John's East said Grand Banks was an international
Supply-Fisheries
shoal. That is true; but the trouble is that there are not enough Canadian boats on that shoal to get our share of the fish, and that will be the position until we have more boats. So I think by granting additional licences to trawlers we will increase the earning power of the fishermen of the maritimes, and put them in a very much better position.
The senior member for Halifax asked if we thought our proposal concerning draggers would increase the productivity of that area. We most certainly think it will. He also spoke about the rosefish, which is new to the New England states. We have some, though not very many, on the Atlantic coast. The bottom is rough where these fish are obtained, and we do not allow our trawlers or draggers close to the shore, so we really have no means of taking them except in very small quantities. They are not a fish that will take any kind of lure or bait.
The hon. member also asked concerning the advisability of oceanographic studies. I would certainly agree with what he said and would hope that at least one university in the maritime provinces and perhaps the university of British Columbia would take this matter into consideration, and also that they would establish classes in fish engineering.
Those are two things that are sadly lacking, and we expect to get these trained men for our services. The hon. member for Charlotte said that this industry would become a major industry. It all depends on the way you think about it, I suppose, because it is a major industry now, if the hours of work mean anything. It is all worth while, however, and I have the greatest confidence in it.
The hon. member for Fort William asked about cookbooks, and suggested that we send 100 to each of the members. He did not suggest them as Christmas cards; but with an autograph on them, they ought to make good advertising for the Department of Fisheries.
Some concern has been shown about the extensive fishing on the Grand Banks. I understand that the latest scientific survey shows no depletion. Will the minister corroborate that?

I am advised that up to the present time there is no indication of depletion of the Grand Banks. I might also say that last fall there was a meeting of some nine countries in Washington to consider the North Atlantic treaty on fishing, that is for survey purposes. There will be another meeting shortly, I expect, and that will

In presenting these estimates, the minister has impressed me as being a man with a purpose. I am glad to see that a man with a purpose is in charge of this department. We Social Credit members are from areas where fishing is not a major industry, but we like those who come from the fishing constituencies to know they have our hearty support. We have not said much, but we have felt a great deal. We are desirous of giving them our hearty co-operation, just as we know they have been desirous of giving us co-operation when we wrestle with the great problems which confront us, as we all work together to build a better Canada.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
I should like to say a few words on this item. Before I do so, however, as the second member from British Columbia to take part in this fisheries debate, I should like to compliment the minister on the new program he has outlined, and to tell the members of the house that we members from British Columbia bask a little in the reflected glory which has come to us now because the minister has inaugurated so sensible a program for the development of our fisheries resources. The only thought, of course, which occurs to us is that if the governments of Canada had not waited eighty years to appoint their first British Columbian as minister of fisheries, progress might have been speeded up considerably.
The attitude of the minister reflects the extremely progressive outlook of the British Columbia fishing industry and the British Columbia fishermen. If the minister can imbue that spirit in the east, in those places to which the hon. member for St. John's West referred as the backward areas, I think the whole industry will benefit.
Great emphasis has been placed on conservation in the fishing industry. Effective conservation depends in large measure upon effective enforcement of the fishing laws. It is for this reason I am on my feet today. I have received a brief from the fishermen of the principal fishing town of my riding, protesting against the continuation of the practice of illegal sunken-net fishing for codfish. We in British Columbia speak so much about our salmon industry that there may be a tendency for people to forget our other fish. We catch halibut, tuna, cod and several species of ground fish in large quantities. The cod
[Mr. Mayhew.l
is the blue ling cod. It represents quite a source of income to fishermen generally. It is caught by hand lines, using small fish as bait.
There are several other means of catching these fish, which are ground fish, one of which is the use of a sunken net. This means a net hanging along the floor of the sea like a curtain, to intercept all types of ground fish. This method of fishing is illegal, except that in various parts of the province it is permitted for catching dogfish, which are a scavenger fish of no value except for the oil from their livers. This is a very easy method of catching all ground fish, including codfish, but the use of the sunken net to catch cod has always been illegal. Sunken nets are not allowed because they destroy so much of the fish. They catch not only the mature fish, but the immature fish which could have been thrown back if they were caught on a hand line. Moreover, the poacher who breaks the law in season is not too much concerned about fishing out of season either, and fishes when the greatest harm can be done, which is during the spawning season.
The fishermen in my riding are protesting about the slackness of enforcement of the law against sunken-net fishing for cod, and the small penalties imposed upon these fishermen when they are caught. I appreciate the fact that normally imposition of the penalty is not within the prerogative of a minister. But on the west coast of British Columbia, as I have said before, there are so many instances in which the department of Fisheries is policeman, prosecutor and judge, that it has a greater measure of control over penalties than any other department. Strict enforcement should not be difficult.
It is easy to recognize a sunken net, because it is so different from the ordinary net used to catch salmon. Salmon gill nets hang from wooden floats, like a curtain from the surface of the water, and they are kept vertical by light lead weights along the bottom edge. A sunken cod net is made up of long narrow strips of old salmon net. Large weights are placed along the bottom and small floats are used so that it sinks to the bottom but remains upright. A fisherman who has in his possession one of these long narrow nets, heavily weighted, is obviously in possession of a sunken net. The standard excuse of a man who is found in possession of a sunken net is that he had been using it in an authorized area. When a fisherman returns from an authorized area it would not be very difficult for him to report to the nearest patrol officer and get his sunken net registered. The patrol officers would know where these sunken nets were, and could easily check on their use.

The next thing to which I should like to refer is the use of otter trawls in the gulf of Georgia. These trawls are most destructive to all types of ground fish, because they are not selective. They catch the mature fish, the immature fish and the spawning fish. They also damage and destroy fish in the process of catching them. The fishermen in my riding, in the interests of conservation, urge the minister not to permit the further use of these otter trawls.

I should like to commend the minister on his statement today, and I join with the other British Columbia members in saying that we are not at all surprised at the capacity he has shown in this post. It is merely indicative of his success in other fields before he came to the House of Commons.
There is one matter I should like to bring to the attention of the house; I have already taken it up with the department. I should like to read to the minister an article that appeared in the press and was sent to me from my riding. It refers to this law-enforcement problem. The headline is, "Heavy penalties are imposed." It reads as follows:
Edward Joseph, John Manson and Felix Thomas were sentenced to pay a fine of $200 each or to spend sixty days in jail by Magistrate T. Patterson last week.
The case was the outcome of charges laid by the fisheries department against the three for having fish in their possession illegally, and obstructing a fisheries guardian in the performance of this duties. The latter charge was not pressed.
Incidentally the article also states that one of the prisoners has arranged to pay his fine, and the other two have left for the sunny vale of Oakalla prison farm. It is getting close to the Christmas season, and the harshness of these penalties has amazed me. I do not know what the fishermen of the maritime provinces would have to do before they would have a penalty such as that imposed upon them. As the minister well knows, the west coast of Vancouver island has been closed to seining this fall, in the interests of conservation, and with that course I have no quarrel. It seems to me, however, that this is an unnecessarily harsh sentence to impose upon native people where their only means of livelihood has been taken away from them. Only $41 worth of fish were involved in this seizure. As a matter of fact, their conviction depended almost entirely on circumstantial evidence.
It was maintained by the departmental officers out there that you could not catch cohoe salmon with a spoon, that they would have to be netted at this time of the year. That may or may not be true. I am not 45781-178j
Supply-Fisheries
trying to argue the merits of the case as to whether the men were guilty or not; but it seems to me that under the circumstances the penalty that was imposed on them is unnecessarily harsh and severe. If the minister would be kind enough to do so, I should like him to take this matter up with his officials and look into all the circumstances surrounding the case. Then if he feels as I do, that an unduly severe penalty has been imposed, I would hope that he would take it up with the attorney general of the province of British Columbia and see if some part of this fine cannot be remitted. The least we can do is to see that these two native Indians out there do not spend their Christmas in prison.

The statement
made by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Gibson) reminds me of something that I should like to bring to the attention of the Department of Fisheries. Nearly every year in Charlotte county at the opening, on November 15, of the lobster season, which is the fall season, the fishermen will find the day of the 14th to be a fine day. At that time of the year it is hard to depend on the weather. If their traps are ready, along in the late part of the afternoon and early in the evening, they will try-as they have done in the past and as they will do in the future-to get these traps on the fishing grounds in order to start on the 15th. On many occasions I have known fisheries patrol boats to go out late in the afternoon or early evening of the 14th and find these traps on the fishing grounds. I have a bit of criticism to offer here.
Quite a long statement appeared in the Montreal Standard just recently saying that the fisheries department destroy the gear that belongs to the fishermen of the province of New Brunswick. I think perhaps that if some other way were found of disposing of fishermen's nets, traps or whatever gear it might, be, instead of destroying them, it would leave a much better feeling with the people who are engaged in that industry. As to a fisherman who is overanxious and puts his traps out on the 14th, and they are found by an employee of the fisheries department, I would suggest that if a heavy fine were imposed rather than the destruction of his gear it would be a great deal better for all concerned. My reason for making that statement is this. A man may have 100 or 150 traps. He puts them out on the 14th. If an employee of the fisheries department destroys those traps, that man is not going to operate during that season. He may have a wife and four or five children. We do not know his circumstances. I

Supply-Fisheries
believe it is entirely wrong for any department to destroy property. In other words, if something were seized by the customs department-we will say a car or whatever it might be-it is not taken out and burned; it is offered for sale. When traps are found that are being fished illegally, even though it is just a few hours before the legal season would open, I believe there could be found some other way of penalizing that fisherman than by destroying what he has to make a living with.
There is one other thing I want to bring to the minister's attention while I am on my feet, and it has been pointed out to him on previous occasions. The hon. member for Comox-Alberni mentioned illegal fishing out in his district. The crew of patrol boats on the Pacific coast in many cases are paid a living allowance while on board those boats. It may be that there is a good deal of patrolling and they have to work seven days a week; I do not know. But that same situation does not prevail in the maritime provinces. I have repeatedly asked for an explanation as to why patrol boats on the Pacific coast should provide living accommodation and food for the crew of the boat when the same thing does not apply on the Atlantic coast boats. I know of one particular patrol boat in my riding whose crew will be away two and three weeks ait a time; they have to pay their own living expenses while on board the boat and keep a family at home. I think that is unfair. I believe the rule that applies on the Pacific coast should also apply on the Atlantic coast. I do not believe any line should be drawn between them. I believe that any crew of a patrol boat that is obliged to be away from home should be given the cost of living while on board that boat.

I just wanted to ask the minister a question, but before doing so I also want to express my appreciation, as a maritimer, of what is being done in connection with the fisheries. I rather hesitate to say anything about it after listening to such men as the hon. member for Charlotte, who has been connected with fishing all his life and certainly is an expert in that matter. Listening to the discussion here this afternoon, however, one would think that the fishing industry was in splendid condition. But I have heard that the markets for fish are not the best. We know that you can sell lobster and other specialized varieties, but in general I think that the markets are not good, and I think it would be wrong to give the country the impression that, so far as the fishermen are concerned, the markets are in the best of condition. I think the minister

is to be commended for trying to improve the markets, and I certainly hope that he succeeds.
The question I wished to ask was in connection with the difficulties that have arisen -in the Northumberland strait between the fishermen and the law enforcement officers: what is the situation down there now? Are there more patrol boats or is there still a sort of civil war going on in that section of the country?

We have provided or are providing for three extra patrol boats for that district and we hope we will catch up with it. There has been a good deal of poaching going on this year both on the east and west coasts. To be perfectly honest, I have not much sympathy with those who have been doing it.

May I ask the
minister a question?
Yes.
Has poaching been carried on extensively in the bay of Fundy, or on the west side of the bay of Fundy?

No, it has not. But it seems as though every time a man who has been poaching or illegally fishing is caught, he seems to get quite a host of friends right away, and they come along and use all their influence. To hear some hon. members talking about the accused, they all seem to have large families; and I would not be surprised if they had three or four wives and that all the neighbours were depending on what they bring in from the sea. Where we have this illegal fishing, if we are going to stop it I think we must at some point be quite drastic about it. I do not think one needs to be drastic very often in order to make it effective. I do not want to be the judge. I am not the judge. As the Minister of Justice said the other day, we intend to make a change next year in our act so that the magistrate will have complete authority. He has complete authority now but the boats are confiscated and are turned over to us. He does not know whether we are going to turn them back, or going to sell them or what we are going to do. The result is that the magistrate will probably give a small fine, thinking that the balance of the punishment is going to come in the loss of the man's gear. Personally, I do not think that is right. The gear is his living and I think that if he is worth anything, it should go back to him and that the magistrate should be in a position to impose a maximum fine for the offence, whether it is a first, second or third one. I hope we shall be able to do that next year, and it will save us all a great

Supply-Fisheries
deal of worry. I hope by that means we shall be able to stamp out some of this illicit fishing. I shall look up the report immediately in respect to what the hon. member said and see what can be done with it. In that case the fine seems to be fairly heavy. I understand that there are several offences in addition to the offence of illegal fishing.
Are these three boats to remain in the area permanently or are they temporary?
They will be there permanently.

Again I should like to ask the minister to indicate whether he believes it is right to destroy fisherman's gear when he is found to be fishing out of season? Has the minister any sympathy with the destruction of fisherman's gear?

The situation there is that our inspectors are out in rather small boats. They pick up a number of lobster traps. The boat can only hold a certain number of lobster traps. If they were not destroyed they would have to come in, land the traps and go out again. In a good many instances the lobster traps are destroyed at sea where they are seized. It is done because the boats are not large enough to bring them in.

The boats that are on patrol in Charlotte county are sufficiently large to take care of forty or fifty lobster traps. When these traps are found the night before the legal season is to open, the rope, the traps and everything are destroyed. I believe that is a condition which the fisheries department should look into very carefully. As I said before, the owner of those traps may have a wife and four or five children. Lobster fishing is his only means of making a living during that season. Winter is coming on. Before the gear that belongs to him is destroyed, very careful consideration should be given to taking it ashore and at least giving him a chance to buy it back, or impose a fine which would perhaps convince him that he should not do it again.
With respect to the appointment of these guardians or fishery patrolmen, are the Royal Canadian Mounted Police employed in this work on Prince Edward Island as well as the ordinary people?

speechtext: No.
No Royal Canadian Mounted Police are employed?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Fisheries
speechtext: No.
Are they employed by the provincial government in fish protection?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Fisheries
speechtext: I cannot answer that question with any degree of authority, but in some instances I believe members of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police are engaged by the provincial authorities for some of their protection work.

I should like to give the hon. member for Charlotte a little information. In May or July of last year in one part of the country fishermen were fishing a little before the opening of the season or a little after, I do not know which it was now, and they were fined around $20 by the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. They caught them in the act. They took their gear from them, but since it was election time in that locality the fine was returned and all their expenses.
I was afraid of that.

105.	Oyster and clam culture, $73,700.

I want to find out something about the tariff on clams going into the United States. On the Pacific coast they ship into the United States a clam called the razor clam. That clam goes into that country under a 10 per cent duty on the Canadian selling price. But when you come to the Atlantic coast, where we have an abundance of clams, you run up against practically an embargo when you ship clams into the United States. There is a tariff of 35 per cent on the United States selling price. Can the minister give me any information on that, or can he find out whether there is a difference of from 10 per cent to 35 per cent on the valuation, which makes it almost impossible for a shipper in the maritime provinces to establish a sales price in the United States because he has to pay a duty on whatever the customs of the United States say their selling price is? On top of that 35 per cent is added.

I have not all the answers to the tariff. I do not know what the items are or what the rate is, but we shall look into it and see what we can do about it. What the hon. member referred to applies to a number of items in the United States tariff.

In the Northumberland strait around Prince Edward Island we have perhaps as good oyster waters as can be found anywhere in the world. The information I have is that the oyster industry has not increased in recent years as it should have. From time to time the department has sent out reports of the great possibilities in the culture of oysters and of the large number

I should like a report from the minister as to the progress that is being made. The estimate for this service has been increased by $22,000. The appropriation in the main estimates is $73,700.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Fisheries
speechtext: In reply to the hon. member for Cumberland I might point out that the department, through its biological board, is doing everything possible to stimulate production of oysters. At the present time the greatest problem is the production of seed for the growth of oysters. I may say that the department and the board are doing their very utmost to carry on experiments and generally improve oyster development in the maritime provinces.

Can the parliamentary assistant inform the committee what progress has been made in the county of Cumberland, in the Malagash district and the Wallace district which have excellent natural oyster waters? I understand that artificial beds have been established there, which have been looked after for a number of years. I should like to know what progress has been made and what production has been obtained from some of these artificially cultivated waters.

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I am sorry to inform the hon. member for Cumberland that although we have established a station in his constituency I have not before me a copy of the report. The production for Northumberland strait in 1946 was 3,100 barrels, in 1947 it was 2,400 and in 1948 it was 3,500.

I am making my last speech this session on the committee stage of these bills. I hope we shall be able to close by Thursday night. I speak now for many reasons in connection with this work on divorce. I was a member of the private bills committee of the House of Commons for many years past and I wish to object to our being asked to pass these bills. I am a humble member of the Church of England.
I believe that we should have some better and fairer consideration of this great problem. The problem is not ours. It has arisen since confederation. I wish to refer to two or three matters with regard to these bills tonight, and as to the way we do this business.
In the first place I wish to say this with regard to these particular bills. I am going to speak for only a few minutes. I do not wish to talk the bills out; far from it. I wish to raise a great problem in this committee about this question which is causing

such wide differences of opinion among the people of this country. I have sat as a member of the private bills committee for many years past since I entered the house. While I believe it is desirable that we should close up as soon as possible, I wish to direct the attention of the committee for only a few minutes this evening to this question. Divorce is a canker in the state. It follows every great war. The Addington administration faced it away back in 1801 after the Peace of Amiens. Then the two Pitts faced the same problem. In connection with this work I might say that when the Constitutional Act was passed in 1791 we adopted in this country so much of the law as was adapted to our circumstances, with the result that after the Constitutional Act of 1791 we copied the common law of England in this country.
Divorce, I repeat, is a canker in the state. There is no doubt about that. The church to which I belong does not believe in it. I am only a humble member. While I am a Protestant I have great respect for the other Christian churches which labour so hard for the good of the people of this country.
In the first place, the principle is all wrong. Why should I be asked to pass all these bills in the manner indicated? I doubt if any other hon. members who had sat as long as I have as a member of the private bills committee would put up with it any longer. Why are we asked to pass these bills without any evidence before us? I wish to point out this fact. I was a member of the committee for a great many years. At the Lambeth conference in England a commission was appointed to study this question in the old country. The members of the Church of England believe in the injunction, "Those whom God hath joined together, let no man put asunder", and I think it is a matter of practical good sense. The Right Hon. and Most Rev. Bishop Wand, as many hon. members know, succeeded Bishop Winnington-Ingram, who has many relatives in Ontario and throughout Canada. Bishop Ingram was the great bishop of London who worked so hard among the poorer classes in the London district for many years. He was succeeded by Bishop Wand who is the present Bishop of London and a member of the House of Lords. He was appointed only recently, and he made an address in Toronto on this question. As I said in the spring session in this house, he was appointed after a great deal of study of this problem. Who suffers as a result of this procedure? I contend it is the duty of the state to look after the wives and the children. Why should they be left, as the right reverend gentleman said in Toronto
Private Bills-Divorce
in an interview? He also preached on other matters in St. James Anglican cathedral in Toronto. The Bishop of London has found that divorce is a canker in the state, that it results in the state having to look after those who suffer. The women and the children of those who are divorced suffer every year as a consequence of these divorce bills. It follows every war. The present Bishop of London has entered on a tour of America. As I said last spring, he has made a great study of this particular problem. I know that the members of the other Christian churches in this country and many of those who are not members of those churches have also done the same thing.
On October 18, 1949, I said, as reported at page 908 of Hansard:
In the church to which I belong, as a humble member-and that is the Church of England-the belief is this: those whom God has joined together, let no man put asunder. That was the principle of the conference in England for a great many years. Recently a commission appointed by the houses of parliament has been considering this whole problem. It is presided ever by the Right Hon. and Right Reverend William Charles Wand, Bishop of London, who succeeded Bishop Winnington-Ingram. Over there, because of the way the country has been devastated by war, and for other reasons, the desire seems to be to extend the principle of divorce to include a great many things that were not considered before as grounds for it; one of these is desertion, and there are seven or eight other matters connected with it. I was glad to hear some of the members here tonight speak on this matter.
Let me say this one thing further. In my humble opinion the state should do something to look after the wives and the children. Every state has people of this type. After every war it has these people and they are a direct charge on the municipality. I know that because I was head of a municipality. I know that they become a charge on the municipality not only for school purposes but for housing and many other matters like that. I believe that the time is coming when we should have some other system adopted by parliament for this work. When I was on that committee I noticed that we knew nothing about the bills. There is a principle of Roman law to the effect that marriage is a contract. The common law of England has been largely copied from Roman law. That has been the principle which has been adopted in this country also. It seems to me that we should provide a better system accordingly.
In connection with this matter I want to point out that there is in existence a registration system. While I admit that it cannot be so in the province of Quebec, there is a registration system operated by the provinces. For what? For deaths and marriages. They have a register with the town or village clerk to that effect. In a great many of the provinces that law regarding these matters might prevail also; but in Quebec I admit that there is a different principle involved. No one wants to change their law. Far from it. I would never try to change their law because I believe that the majority of the people are entitled to have their say themselves.
In conclusion, may I say that I think we should have a conference of the two houses of parliament, because it has been largely the prerogative of the Senate to hear and examine witnesses and all that

Private Bills-Divorce sort of thing. I do not believe in the system. In the United States, after many wars, divorce is becoming a canker in almost every state. As I say, it follows largely as a result of wars. There is a registration system for deaths and marriages in existence in some of the provinces. I do not see why that system cannot be adopted. No doubt a different system would be required1 in the great province of Quebec. The archbishop who was investigating this question is travelling in the United States at the present time. He succeeded Bishop Winnington-Ingram, the great bishop of London, England. He is visiting the United States at the present moment and is going into all these questions. He recognizes that the divorce laws should be extended to include desertion.
I think there is something to be said in favour of that. I do not wish to occupy the time of the committee any further, Mr. Chairman. On page 224 of the Canada Year Book of last year, under the heading of "Vital Statistics", the following appears:
For many years after confederation, the number of divorces in Canada was very small. It was less than 20 in every year before 1900. There were 23 divorces in 1903, 51 in 1909 and 60 in 1913. These numbers were less than 1 per 1,000 of the yearly number of marriages.
One effect of the first world war was to increase the number of divorces. The generally unsettled conditions and the long separation between men on active service and their wives contributed to this increase. Changes in law and procedure which made it easier to obtain divorce was a further factor. At present, Quebec is the only province in which applicants for divorce must secure a private act of parliament.
There were 114 divorces in Canada in 1918 and 608 in 1926; the number had increased to 700 by 1931, 1,570 by 1936 and 2,369 by 1940. In every year since then the number has been higher than in the year before. The figures for the most part cover only final decrees of dissolution of marriage which alone constitute divorces; annulments and legal separations are excluded.
The statistics of dissolutions of marriage were revised in 1941 with the co-operation of the provincial authorities and the clerk of the divorce committee of the Senate of Canada.

The house resumed from Tuesday, November 29, consideration of the motion of Mr. Benidickson for the second reading of Bill No. 119, to incorporate Prairie Transmission Lines Limited, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Maclnnis.

Mr. Speaker, this is the first opportunity I have had to speak on any of these bills. I propose to speak on this one tonight.
In the first place I am in favour of the building of a pipe line. I say "a" pipe line because I believe that only one will be built. If that is so, I do not see any reason for the granting of so many charters for the building of potential pipe lines. We are told that several of these charters are being applied for in order that there may be certain manipulation in regard to financial matters, and that in that respect some of these applications are not what they appear to be on the surface.
I am no judge of that. I am in favour of the building of a pipe line or of pipe lines if, by so doing, there shall be an increase in the public service,-if, for example, it may result in the cheapening of the price of fuel oil and gasoline to those people who require it. The question is: Will the building of this pipe line or any other pipe lines, for that matter, accomplish this object? I have noticed particularly of late in the oil business in western Canada indication of a getting together in the matter of price on the part of the largest oil companies, a procedure which I think is not justified by the ease with which some of the oil is transported.
It is an admitted fact that the building of a pipe line should ease the transportation of fuel. But I wonder whether that will result in a consequent easing of prices and the elimination of what I would call manipulation of prices. In my own city of Saskatoon there are three major oil companies supplying fuel oil to consumers. It was shown that it cost one of those companies eight cents a gallon to transport their oil to a refinery and back to Saskatoon. On the other hand there are two other companies the expenses of which are much different. Yet we find that the final price to the door of the consumer is one and the same.
Prairie Transmission Lines
Furthermore, the city of Regina, which is much farther from Lloydminster, the source of supply, is enjoying a price of 14-6 cents a gallon, while in Saskatoon the consumer is paying 18 cents for fuel oil. I would be more in favour of granting charters to these companies than I am now if I were sure that the easing of the transportation problem would result in lower prices and in less of that sort of price manipulation.
Another thought occurs to me. Will the granting of this charter guarantee that such a pipe line will be built? Again I use as an example my city of Saskatoon, and tell the house about an experience we had. Just before the last war broke out a certain gas company, the name of which I shall not give, received a franchise to transport natural gas to my city of Saskatoon. Some people were so sure they would have this gas that they made arrangements to change their stoves from coal-burning to gas-burning.
The war broke out and, under certain clauses in the franchise, these people were able to get out of their contract during the duration of the war. They had put up a large sum of money with the city as a guarantee. We thought naturally that after the war was over the power granted under the franchise would be exercised. But that has not happened, and since the war Saskatoon has been waiting for its supply of natural gas.
Someone will say, "Is that not a legal matter? These people can be sued and damages collected." I am not learned in legal procedure, but I have learned through my experience that such procedure is somewhat slow and tortuous. Up to the present time Saskatoon has no gas, and so far as I know there is no prospect of getting any.
I give these facts as an example of a franchise which was granted, and nothing done about it. Another feature I should like to mention in regard to pipe lines is that a pipe line, by its very nature, is in itself a transportation system, just the same as is a railway. As such, in my opinion, it should be used by other people in addition to those who have obtained the franchise to construct the pipe line. Therefore one of the first questions I would ask with respect to this or any other pipe line is: Is this pipe line, or is it not, to be a public carrier? We have no guarantee of that.
When we ask such a question we are told that we have to address our question to the board of transport commissioners after the line has been built. I suggest we should address our question in the same manner as we should address the question as to the geographical position of the line-not after it has been built, but before. Another thing

Prairie Transmission Lines I should like to suggest is that as this pipe line is a transportation system, it should be publicly owned. There are certain things about which I am worried in regard to this particular pipe line bill and there are certain questions I should like to ask.
If refineries other than those controlled by the company constructing the pipe line are to have the use of the pipe line, will there be regulations regarding such public service and as to the amount of outside material that may be carried by the pipe line in proportion to the amount of material owned by the company constructing the pipe line? Next, provided the company has or builds refineries along the route of the pipe line sufficient to refine the total capacity of the pipe line, can it then refuse to handle oil transportation for other companies?
Next, if pipe line capacity is allocated on a percentage basis can the company arrange its own chronology as to deliveries? Most hon. members are aware that on the western prairies there is a season of heavy demand for oil and a slack season. Will the company owning a line of this kind be able to use the line for its own purposes during the season of heavy demand and then permit the pipe line to be used by other refineries during the less valuable time?
Can the company insist that the percentage allocated to refineries other than its own shall be delivered on the prairies during the nonagricultural months? Can it be incorporated in the legislation that the percentage delivered to other refineries shall be on a year-round or a day by day or a month by month basis?
The building of this pipe line or of other potential pipe lines is a matter of concern to many organizations in my part of the country. I have the resolution which was sent to me by the trades and labour council of Saskatoon, which reads:
Whereas Canadian natural resources should be exploited for the benefit of all Canadians and Canada should endeavour to become a self-supporting industrial nation having all its resources under its complete control, and
Whereas, it is planned that the proposed pipe line is to be partly built-
This resolution refers to a different pipe line.
-and terminate on American soil making it no longer an all-Canadian enterprise.
Whereas, our dollar has been devaluated and we are spending $200 million annually buying oil from the United States, thus using American dollars, and
Whereas, an all-Canadian route for the proposed pipe line would employ Canadian labour in its construction and maintenance and would largely employ Canadian ships and sailors to transport this oil to the refinery with the prospect of a refinery at the lake-head with all its benefits to Canadian citizens.

As I say, this resolution really refers to another pipe line but I am reading it in order to bring out my point that it is the concern of a great number of Canadian citizens that all of these pipe lines shall be built on Canadian soil. The resolution continues:
Therefore be it resolved, that this Saskatoon trades and labour council urge all its local unions to press the government to make this oil pipe line an all-Canadian route, and
Further be it resolved, that this resolution be forwarded to the Honourable C. D. Howe, Minister of Trade and Commerce, asking him to use his influence with the government to take action to ensure the above undertaking.
They realized that the influence of Mr. Howe with the government is great and perhaps in that regard they are making something of an understatement. To summarize, may I say that I consider these pipe lines should be publicly owned as they concern public transportation. Second, if a pipe line is built it should provide service to companies other than the one building the pipe line. Third, any pipe line should be built on Canadian soil for its entire distance.

Mr. Speaker, in the bill before us tonight for consideration we find an opportunity to renew the debate upon the application to incorporate a gas pipe line company by the name of Prairie Transmission Lines Limited. This company proposes to build a pipe line for the transportation of natural gas from Alberta, through the United States of America, with the primary object of serving the Pacific coast United States cities of Seattle, Tacoma and Portland, with any surplus being made available to Vancouver. We have before us for immediate consideration an amendment to the motion for second reading moved by the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis). This amendment will be found on page 2103 of Hansard of November 22, 1949, and reads:
That Bill No. 119 be not now read a second time but that it be resolved that in the opinion of this house further consideration of this bill should be deferred until the house has been assured that the route of any pipe line built by the proposed company will be laid out so as to serve Canadian requirements before any such pipe line leaves Canadian soil.
I should like to congratulate the hon. member for Vancouver East upon that amendment because better than any speech or words that could have been used it places the issue squarely before us. At this point may I say that I intend to stop in time for a vote to be taken on the amendment. The issue is whether we shall insist on Canadian resources being used first to serve Canadian development, or whether we shall consent to the exploitation and exportation of our resources for the benefit and extension primarily of other interests. That is the

whole question and it seems to me that the issue raised by the amendment goes far beyond the mere question of whether we shall incorporate a company. The issue involves the control and development of Canada's resources.
Those of us who have spoken in opposition to the incorporation of this particular company are doing more than speak against an individual incorporation. I realize that it has been said that there is a filibuster against a private bill, but I would point out that this is the first opportunity that has been afforded the house to debate the method of handling a tremendous new resource which has been made available to the Canadian people. The two private bills which have been before the house this session seeking the incorporation of companies to handle natural gas afford the first opportunity we have had to consider fully the policy that will govern the development, exploitation and transportation of this huge Canadian resource.
Those who are sponsoring the bill before the house tonight have taken the position that we should not oppose the incorporation of this particular company or of the other company that has been before us. They say that is the only principle involved in the bill, whether or not the house is going to grant incorporation to a company in order that it may subsequently make its application to the board of transport commissioners and the government of Alberta for permission to carry gas.
Far more than that is involved in this and the other bill now before the house. But if that were the only principle I would have no hesitation in saying that I am opposed to that principle, because I am opposed to the incorporation by this parliament of any company for the purpose of transporting and supplying to ultimate consumers elsewhere a Canadian natural resource, when the company through the sponsor of the bill will not give the assurance that the route will be through Canada and will serve Canada first.

What about the bill last
year?

When the bill went through last year we knew at the time the company was incorporated that the route would be all-Canadian; but the assurance we have asked for with respect to this bill, as to whether this line will follow an all-Canadian route and serve Canada first, to my knowledge has not been given.

The hon. member speaks of an assurance given in connection with the
Prairie Transmission Lines bill that went through last year. Is it not true that this assurance was given in committee; and is not the hon. member right now preventing this bill from going to committee?

I am coming to that point now, because that assurance, wherever given, was given, and the public statements of the company agreed that it would be an all-Canadian route. On the other hand we have before us a statement by this company which indicates clearly that they do not propose to build their line through Canada. So it does not seem necessary to permit this bill to go to committee in order to establish something which is already established in the advertisements issued by this company.
In his statement in moving second reading the hon. member sponsoring the bill laid before the house the proposition that the route of the company is not involved in this motion. At page 1344 of Hansard for November 1 of this year he said:
I wish to make it clear that the passing of this bill does not in any way establish routes for the transmission lines for this company.
He went on to say:
As I say, as far as federal jurisdiction is concerned, under the direction of this parliament it was ordered in the last session that routes must be decided upon by the board of transport commissioners.
In my submission that statement is not strictly accurate, and I shall deal with it a little later in discussing the general Pipe Lines Act. Then at page 1345 the hon. member went on:
I should like to inform the house that the bill has nothing to do with routes. .
Well, Mr. Speaker, it is perfectly true that the bill before us makes no mention of routes; but the advertising put out by the company does deal with routes, and lays out the route this company proposes to follow. The advertisement appeared in the Calgary Herald of August 11, 1949. I believe it has been read to the house already, so perhaps I need not read it in full, but it sets out that the purpose of the company is to transport or transmit natural and artificial gas and oil in the provinces of Alberta and British Columbia, commencing at a point in the general Calgary area in the province of Alberta and thence to a point in the vicinity of Blairmore in the said province and thence to a point in the vicinity of Kingsgate in the province of British Columbia and thence to the United States of America, leaving Canada at a point at or near Kingsgate in the said province of British Columbia and re-entering Canada in the vicinity of Blaine in the state of Washington. This means that for by far the greater portion of its distance the line would go

Prairie Transmission Lines through the United States; and as we know from other public statements of the company its purpose is primarily to supply those United States Pacific coast cities of which mention has been made already.
So the advertisements and public statements of this company make their object perfectly clear; and it is that object to which I am opposed, for the reasons I have stated. I believe it is our responsibility as members of the Canadian parliament to see to it that Canada's resources are used for Canada's benefit. I do not say we should adopt the selfish attitude of saying, "You cannot have anything of which we have an abundance", but that we should adopt the attitude of saying, "We are going to use our resources for ourselves first, to fulfil our own requirements. Then we shall be willing to export our surplus to you; in fact we shall be willing to co-operate with you in a proper division of our resources". That is not what this bill does. The purpose of this bill is to export the gas to the United States first; then if anything is left over it will be sent back to Vancouver, entirely by-passing the interior areas of British Columbia.
In opposing that principle I should like to lay before the house some words which seem to me to contain a very clear statement of the attitude and sentiments of those who share my opinions in this respect. This statement is contained in the December, 1949, issue of a publication put out by Ross Whittall Limited, of Vancouver. In dealing with natural gas development in this country it says:
Where the railways brought industries during the last half century so should natural gas bring them during the next, for it provides cheap thermal units at a fraction of the cost of transit.
I ask hon. members on all sides, who at least will sympathize with us in the vision we have as to the development of our province and the western half of our nation, to listen to these words:
New towns should grow and, if our province has nearly doubled its population in the last decade, what may be the expectancy of the next? We then foresee the pipe lines providing valuable U.S. dollar exports to central Washington and to the U.S.A. Pacific seaboard and we know that these American populations will not grudge us our contention that first Alberta and then neighbouring Canadian provinces benefit from our newly-found economic stimulant. Geologists are satisfied that there is plenty for all; indeed we believe that one of the largest sources of supply may lie close to recently proved reserves beneath the Peace river block in British Columbia and Alberta. . . . but let us make sure that, wherever we find it, our Canadian natural gas serves and opens up the maximum quantity of our own country before it benefits the neighbouring states of America.
And, Mr. Speaker, the only time and place that responsibility which it is our duty to

exercise here as members of this parliament can be exercised is now, in this House of Commons, in opposing this and other similar bills which seek to export gas first to the United States. If this bill were given approval we would lose control of the gas from here on. It would go to the United States, and from then on would become a United States resource not subject to Canadian control and of no use for the development of Canada.
Some hon. members have said it is not for this parliament to oppose the incorporation of this company, that we should leave it to the Alberta government to decide whether or not the gas will be exported to the United States, that they have the necessary legislation and the necessary machinery. It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, it would be most unfair to impose upon the Alberta government the responsibility of saying whether or not their resources will be exported from Canada. The concern of that government is to make sure there is sufficient of their natural resources left in their province to take care of their own requirements. It is not their concern to prohibit its transportation from that province to the United States. A reading of the Alberta act shows that they are concerned mainly with the preservation of a supply, not the control of where any surplus goes, if there is a surplus, once it leaves the province.
It is said, "Well, leave it to the board of transport commissioners; let them say what the route of the pipe line should be; let that body take the responsibility of saying whether it should be kept in Canada or exported to the United States". I point out to the sponsor of the bill, who made that suggestion, that there is no provision in the Pipe Lines Act which would empower the board of transport commissioners to take that into consideration, in saying whether or not approval shall be given to a company. There is a reference in section 9 of the Pipe Lines Act covering approval of the route, but that act does contemplate the export of gas. It contemplates a gas pipe line going to the international border, and crossing into the United States. It is inherent in the act.
I am sure the sponsor of the bill, who is a lawyer, would agree with me that it would be beyond the powers of the board of transport commissioners to say that, merely because the route contemplates the international transportation of gas, they will not approve the application. The Pipe Lines Act itself contemplates an international gas pipe line. We cannot leave it to the Alberta government; we cannot leave it to the board of transport commissioners to decide whether or not a gas pipe line should serve Canada first before the gas is exported to the United

States. There is only one place where that can be decided under the present set-up, and that is in this parliament. It must be decided, by our insistence as legislators dealing with the matter, that the route should be through Canada. There Is only one way in which we can accomplish that result, and that is by insisting that there be embodied in the act incorporating the company a provision that the route shall pass over Canadian soil, and that the gas shall be used first to supply Canadian needs. Then, the surplus could be exported to the United States.
Did you insist upon that for the company that was here last year?
I have answered my hon. friend with respect to the company that came last year; it undertook to build a Canadian route.
Oh, no.

As I have stated before, I feel that the issue before the house at this time is the issue contained in the amendment moved by the member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis). Before any of these bills be allowed to pass, the sponsor of the bill should give assurance and that assurance should be incorporated in the act itself, that the pipe line will be built across Canadian soil, and the gas will be used first to serve Canadian purposes. Then, we shall gladly share the surplus with the United States. That proposition has been laid clearly before the sponsor, and the persons who seek incorporation of this company, and that assurance has not been given. For the reasons I have stated, and because I feel that in this parliament we must adopt a positive policy for the development of our own resources to build up the western area of our country as an economically powerful unit, and because assurances have not been given, I support the amendment moved by the member for Vancouver East and oppose the bill for which second reading is sought tonight.

This particular matter, which is now before this house, is starting to grip the imagination of the people. I am of the opinion, sir, that our Canadian people should think of it from the point of view which has been brought to their attention for many years, that is the rather broad view which reminds us that, in so far as these particular resources which Providence has given to this country are concerned, we ought not to be hewers of wood and drawers of water for that great magnet to the south of us. We should have that intestinal fortitude to develop our own resources, within our own country, which befits the strong men of the north, who are going to make this country what Providence designed it to be.
Prairie Transmission Lines
Three years ago this month, it was my high privilege to receive a cable from London to go there immediately. The transport division of this government enabled me, although I received the cable on a Friday, to be in Kingsway house, London, within three days. Whilst there-I am talking, Mr. Speaker, about these gas and oil deposits that are in Alberta-my imagination was gripped by the possibilities provided by the gas and oil in Alberta. At that time I was able, sir, to interest some British concerns in those fields.
I see my hon. friend, who is paired with me in the house, smiling. He has a ten million pounds sterling statement under his hands now, sent to him this afternoon, showing the magnitude of this enterprise.
I say to you, Mr. Speaker, that that same organization is working in Calgary, Alberta, today. They have sunk several hundreds of thousands of dollars into that proposition, and they are using thousands of feet of that natural gas to develop and produce a product which is required in this country of ours. This is only one small example of what might be done, if the hon. members in this chamber would only let imagination grip them, and attempt to develop our country. With the help of the know-how of those in Britain, we could develop our own country, and use all the natural products and the natural fuel tn aid in that development.
Let us not continue for the next hundred years, Mr. Speaker, to be hewers of wood and drawers of water for the 140 million people to the south of us. Let us have the intestinal fortitude to develop our own country for our own people, and take full advantage of the possibilities we have in this country.
You have made it; it is nine o'clock.
Before I sit down, I know my time is up, but I want to answer one question that was posed to me today by the senior member for Halifax. I note that he is not in the house at the moment-

The customs and excise divisions have taken over no former employees from the wartime prices and trade board. Some of them may have gone to the taxation division.
They did. I did not suggest that they were taken over by the customs and excise divisions.

That is the item we are discussing at the present time. The general administration item here has to do with the administration of the customs and excise divisions. I do not ask for the breakdown by individual branches; it is just the total I want.
We will give you the total.

We are subject to your ruling, Mr. Chairman, but if we are to have the questions broken down as between these two divisions, I think we shall be at this matter a needlessly long time. Mr. Chairman, since the inception of the department and of the two divisions over thirty years ago-and the customs department is as old as confederation -it has been the custom and the time-honoured tradition to handle the estimates in the way that they are being handled at this time, namely, as of two divisions, and that is the way that I propose to give answers to questions that hon. gentlemen ask. I shall now answer his question with reference to the number of employees. The total number of permanent employees as of the 31st of March, 1949, in the customs and excise divisions was 4,579; temporary employees 1,414; seasonal employees, 237, making a total of 6,230. The largest number of employees is at the different ports-that is, in every town and city where we have a customs and excise tax office.
