Supply-National Revenue
With reference to the first item, the increased expenditure of $177,000 is made up principally by the increase in salaries over a year ago. That amounts to $173,999. Office stationery and supplies amount to $5,000, and travelling $5,000 additional.

I asked the minister whether reclassifications were being made this year. My question was in general; it was not specifically on the first item. Can the minister indicate whether there are reclassifications proceeding in the customs and excise divisions of the department? From the details given in the estimates, a substantial change in the numbers is indicated. One would think that a revision of various classifications was pending.

Not in this department. There is no far-reaching revision or reclassification. Occasionally employees are being made permanent. Our quota of permanent employees is eighty-five per cent, and we are fairly close to the maximum of that quota. The reclassifications go on practically the whole year round, depending upon the length of time an employee has been in the department. No one can be made permanent until he is in the employ of the department for a year. One person might come in in June and another in December, so that from month to month some reclassifications and permanencies are being effected.

Mr. Chairman, I want to ask the minister a set of questions in regard to censorship, particularly censorship of books.
I asked certain questions of the Secretary of State, and at that time the Minister of National Revenue was good enough to say that I should ask them on his estimates and that he would be pleased to answer them.
I have certain ideas in regard to censorship which I shall not inflict upon the committee at this moment, but I shall preface my remarks by saying that I have always had a great deal of difficulty in rending the curtain which has been hung around the censorship branch in this country.
I think, sir, that the idea of censorship is more efficiently applied to the working of the department than it is to the material to which it is supposed to be applied. I opened this inquiry a year or two ago by addressing to the minister or to his department certain questions on the order paper. At that time there was a lack of information which astounded me, and encouraged me to pursue my inquiry. I have not yet received the answers to my questions, and I am going to ask one or two of the minister tonight so 
that he may have an opportunity to answer them, and I may be allowed to comment as we go along.
When I broached the matter first my concern was to find who was the one man in this country responsible for the final adjudication upon a borderline case-that is to say, who has the final say in whether a book shall be admitted to the country or not. I did not expect to get the name. That is not the point. I want to know what official it is in the department. I instituted my inquiry a couple of years ago, and for personal reasons I was not able to pursue it at that time. I insisted that that man should be a person who by education, background, experience and knowledge of literature would be competent to censor books coming into the country or books which are produced in this country.
I do not want to give the impression that I am in favour of censorship. On the whole I am not, except in the cases which were covered by the bill of the hon. member for Kamloops, to which I gave my heartiest support. Now we are talking about a different thing. We are talking about the censorship of adult reading, and the keeping out of this country of books which perhaps should be admitted, and the allowing of books into this country which perhaps should be kept out.
I have maintained, and I challenge contradiction-I can do this because the statement has never been denied-that this condition of affairs means that the men who in the past have been responsible for this censorship were not efficient, in the respects which I have outlined, to do that particular job. That is my general charge. The minister has the facts, and I shall listen with interest to what he has to say in that particular.
To go into the circumstances of this matter, let me say that the department and the officials in charge of censorship looked upon my inquiries, as I see it, in altogether too affable and casual a manner. They looked upon them as, after all, a matter of not much importance-"after all, any customs officer can censor a book." I have that, sir in the actual words of the gentleman in charge of that particular job, astounding as it may sound to many.
I shall not mention anyone's name, because I have no purpose of that sort. I am only anxious that if we are going to have censorship in this country we shall have efficient censorship, and done by people who understand what they are doing.
I d i not think for one moment that people can be agreed upon this matter. One man's meat is another man's poison. I know censorship is a tremendously difficult operation, and

that is the reason I want people with the necessary background to make wise decisions in the matter. That, I claim, has not been done.
In regard to this particular inquiry, I asked certain questions of the department. I said, "Who is this man? What are his qualifications? What is his education? What is his background?" The answers I received were so ludicrous that I blush to mention them to the house. I heard, for instance, that he had some twenty or thirty years' experience in the customs and excise branch-as if that would make him a literary critic. That is the first one.
The gentleman himself said at that time that he was only a temporary employee substituting for an elderly gentleman who was on leave of absence preliminary to his retiring from the service. That in itself was a peculiar situation-a temporary employee. He said he was going to be replaced, he hoped, by a permanent employee.
Perhaps I might say a word or two before I ask my question. I had intended to do this later, but I might as well give the house the rest of the story. This gentleman was interviewed by a member of the press and asked how he regarded this particular occupation of censor of Canadian literature? The pressman said this gentleman was an affable person who confessed that a daily diet of certain types of literature was not at all to his taste. He said he was filling in until the regular appointment was made.
One of my questions is as to whether that regular appointment has been made of a permanent person, and whether that person has the qualifications to which I have referred. This gentleman went on to say further, "It does not require any particular training to tell a bad book." I do not know whether the gentleman was suggesting that perhaps he could smell it. He said, "You do not need a lot of education to spot a bad book." That was his point of view in regard to censorship, a Mrs. Grundy point of view-nothing at all about the quality of the literature, nothing at all about the necessary realism that perhaps should appear in a novel to make it realistic, as distinct from the typical pornographic thing written with a deliberate purpose of creating a best seller. He had no conception whatever of those things.
He said-and I am quoting his words to the newspaper reporter of the Regina Leader-Post; and that reporter may be in the gallery tonight for all I know-
You do not need a great deal of education to know whether a book is bad or not when you read it.
Supply-National Revenue
Then he goes on to discuss certain readers. May I for the information of the committee state-and perhaps I shall anticipate the minister-that there is a certain group of readers who are supposed to read these particular pieces of literature and then hand them on to this final mogul, whoever he is. He makes the final decision.
These readers, by the way, are not all men; I understand, and the minister will correct me if I am wrong, that the chief censor in this country is really a lady. However he said this:
They had no special training for their work- That is interesting.
-but have had years of experience in the job. When appointed they had no special recommendations qualifying them for the position. They were appointed by the civil service commission.
That might help them. The gentleman went on to say, when pressed in regard to making a decision, and to what extent he was influenced by the decision of these particular readers, that he usually concurred in the findings of the readers. With his qualifications I suggest that that perhaps is quite probable.
And either bans or approves importation of the bock in question ... If our appraiser is doubtful about certain passages you can pretty well depend upon it that they are bad.
Well, sir, to me this whole thing is astounding, in this day and age, when Canada is growing up and when Canada is more and more asserting herself as a nation, when Canada is more and more trying to encourage the development of her own writers in this country.
I could go on, because I made an investigation into this matter. I have a thick file upon it. I have statements from people and I have communicated with authors and with some persons bearing very famous names which would be recognized at once if I mentioned them in this chamber tonight. I have their opinions in the matter.
Then the matter of foreign language books comes up. How is a decision made as to whether foreign language books are to be admitted to this country? I remember asking a young mountie who was looking for seditious literature if the Ladies Home Journal was all right. He said he did not know, that he would have to look up the list and let me know later.
That is exactly the type of thing one would expect from the average customs officer, when it comes to censoring literature. The thing is just foolish. Literature is being handled like liquor, tobacco, sugar or something being brought across the line. How do we expect these men to become competent in the matter

Supply-National Revenue of handling foreign languages? As a matter of fact we did have several translators after the war. But now I understand from the Secretary of State, as I elicited by questioning him the other night, that these translators are practically all men who translate the two official languages of the country, English and French.
I have not received any satisfactory answer as to the number or the capabilities of the foreign language translators. A book is presented to a customs officer, I presume. I simply say this, that I do not think a customs officer is competent to handle that situation. The easiest thing for him to do is to admit the book and be done with it. The alternative is to be doubtful about it and send it up to the readers at Ottawa. The readers look around and find some passage in it which may be doubtful. They submit it to this final person, whoever he is, and he makes the final decision. And so some customs and excise officer in this country is telling me what I shall read and shall not read. I object to that.
Perhaps there is no use getting upset about all this. X could tell the committee a good deal more about it, and it is a sad story. You see, we have only one or two foreign language translators to handle the literature of all other languages, except French and English. I appeal to hon. members: What efficiency can one expect under the system I have described?
The minister may say that I make false accusations and these things are not true. All right; let the minister say so. I have been asking his department to say so for two or three years. One of the faults I find with the genial minister is that he does not trouble about these things; he seems to think that it is not of any importance. May I suggest to him that this is something which is perhaps a little over the head of this particular departmental official. This man is not a competent judge as to what I shall or shall not read.
These foreign books come in, and I am sure that some of them are all right and some of them are all wrong, but nobody knows. I have bought books that were on the banned list-and by the way I should like to ask the minister whether that list has been revised in the last forty years. I should like to ask hirfi if Bellamy's "Looking Backward" is still on the list. I thought they took it off, but if they have not, it will indicate the kind of-censorship we have had in this country.
I have some constructive as well as destructive criticism to make. I do not think that any one man, particularly the ordinary customs officer, should have the responsibility

of making the final decision in borderline cases. I have recommended that a committee be appointed to help in this matter. Let the official have the name of being the censor, but he could be assisted by this committee made up of people who know something about the matter.
I think I have said enough, but there are some questions I should like to get in before the clock overtakes me. First of all, I should like to ask the minister whether the gentleman-I have not named him-who has been described as an affable, middle-aged man who was on a temporary basis, has been replaced by a permanent official who is capable of doing this work.

Ever since confederation there has been a law on the statute book that literature that is immoral, indecent and seditious shall be prohibited from entry into the country. I shall not keep the hon. gentleman in suspense any longer; I will tell him that the duty of enforcing that law devolves upon the minister in charge of the department. If there is a mystery man at all in connection with censorship, I plead guilty to that indictment. So far as Mr. Merriam goes, who has given him information with reference to censorship-

On a question of privilege, I have never seen Mr. Merriam in my life, nor have I ever communicated with him, nor have I ever received any information from him. the last time I asked the minister that question he did not give me the information that he was responsible. He said that a certain man in his department gave the final decision. In fact the last time I asked the minister that question he said: "Of course I do not do the work; the hon. member for Saskatoon city must know that we have a staff". I can turn that up in Hansard. I am glad to know-or am I?-that the minister is now the official responsible.

The hon. member asked me a question with reference to the former censor, whether he was still doing it and whether he was in the employ of the department. I was going to say no; that Mr. Merriam, who for some time did that work, is no longer in the employ of the department.

The minister said that I had received information from Mr. Merriam, a man whom I have never seen in my life. I can give the minister the man's name as I have it here. I shall send it over, because I do not like mentioning civil servants in the committee; but apparently the minister has no such scruples.

As I say, the responsibility belongs to the minister, but the minister

cannot personally censor the books, and he depends upon his officials. The general executive assistant of the department is the one who has that responsibility, and he has persons to assist him with the reading and censorship of these books. If translations are required, and there are translators available in the Department of the Secretary of State, their services are obtained. If they cannot meet the requirements, then people outside the department are used.
I suggest that it would be folly for the department to have full-time officials who would have as little work to do as they would have to do in censoring books written in other languages for which entry into this country might be sought. I suggest that you do not have to be a great literary critic to tell the difference between decency and filth. I have looked at a number of these books, and without reading them very far I could see that they were not the type of literature that should be let loose in this country where everybody can read it. Just the other day a ban was placed on crime comics, and it is now a criminal offence for them to be sold in this country. Much of the literature that seeks admission to this country is so filthy and so immoral, and some of it so seditious, that the department would be doing a great disservice to Canada to allow such trash to come into the country.

I have no disagreement with the minister as to crime comics; I thought that would be understood by the minister. I think my actions will back up what I say, because I supported the bill against crime comics. Secondly, I do not think there is any need to have a lot of people skilled in literature on full-time pay in the department. It would be possible to have committees to read this literature without having people on fulltime pay.
I have not been told yet whether there is a man definitely in charge of this particular work, and who is responsible for it. I should like to know also how many readers are reading this type of literature at the moment. I am not talking about crime comics or the other filthy things that were dealt with by the bill. sponsored by the hon. member for Kamloops.
I simply gave that as an example.

I am referring to what might be termed legitimate novels. I admit that some of them should be kept out of the country, and I want them kept out, but I do not want those that should be let in to be kept out. Such books should not be kept out because of the attitude of a censor who
Supply-National Revenue does not know his business and who, in the case of doubt, refuses to admit a book. I think that has been the attitude of the department up until the present time. When I started my inquiry there were three readers in the department; is that the position at the moment?

There is not a single person whose sole duty is censorship. There is a sufficient staff to meet the requirements with reference to reading and censorship of these books, but this need varies from time to time. The responsibility is in no way put upon the collectors of customs at the ports of entry. If there is reason to suspect that any literature coming over the border at any of the ports is indecent, immoral or seditious, such books are sent to the head office in Ottawa for determination as to whether or not they should be allowed entry.

The question I asked the minister was perfectly straight and plain, but perhaps he did not understand it. I did not ask whether these people were full-time employees, whether they were customs officers or anything else. I asked how many people are engaged at times in reading these books -that is, both ladies and gentlemen-to decide whether or not they are proper reading matter for the people of Canada. That was my question. It is easy to answer. How many; one, two, three, or what number?
The number is three or more, depending upon the requirements.

Then I want to ask a further question. I think we are pretty clear that a book published in the United States is subject to examination by customs officers at the border. If the customs officer is in doubt he sends the book to Ottawa. Here it is scrutinized by the reader, who submits it to somebody for a final decision, and that decision is made. There have been instances, of course, where ten thousand or more copies of these books have been distributed throughout the country before the decision was made. I have known of books which were refused admittance at one customs port but which could be bought at the next town, where they had been allowed in; but that is just by the way.
Now we have the number of readers; there are three. I take it these are the same three who were in charge a couple of years ago, one of whom is the lady I mentioned, who I was given to understand was the main censor in Canada. This gentleman who was so long in charge has already stated that he accepted without reserve the advice of these readers, and that is my point. It was

Supply-National Revenue the reader who was making the final decision; the higher official was simply a customs officer who said, "Well, all right, if that is your choice." Now we have had the procedure in connection with books coming from outside Canada. Let us get at what is done in connection with books published within Canada. I take it that no books published in Canada are censored at all, unless information is laid by some individual or by an official in a provincial government who, after a book has been in circulation, discovers it and submits it to Ottawa for adjudication. Would I be correct in that?

We have absolutely nothing to do with books published in Canada. These customs regulations have to do entirely with the entry of books from foreign countries. As head of the department I take full responsibility for the final say as to whether these books enter or are prohibited, and I intend to do that until some better system of censorship is set up, if that is required, by the Canadian parliament.

That is exactly what I am advocating, that some better system of censorship should be set up by the Canadian government. That is why I am criticizing the system we have now. The minister says he is the final adjudicator, that he is the man who decides with respect to a borderline book. With all due respect to the minister-let it be understood that there is nothing personal in this, because the minister knows I have all respect for him and his ability-I suggest I would rather have censorship, that is to say the final adjudication, in the hands of a committee chosen to do that particular work, not necessarily on a permanent basis. Further I would ask the minister how many books are on the banned list at the moment. I am not talking about love story magazines or crime comics, or that sort of thing. What is the approximate number of books on that list?
I cannot give the figure accurately, but I am told it is in the neighbourhood of three or four hundred.
Perhaps the minister could tell me how many books have been banned during the past year, if he has that information.

During the period from
April 1, 1949, to November 30, 1949, some eighty books and seventeen publications, in English and French, were prohibited. No foreign language books or publications have been prohibited during that period.

Carried.
CMr. Knight.]

It is not carried. If my hon. friend would like to take up where I leave off I should be delighted. This is something I believe should be ventilated, and I propose to ventilate it. If my hon. friend desires to assist I should be glad to hear his opinion on the matter; otherwise I suggest he leave this matter to me. Now I ask the minister how often this list of banned books is revised. You know, as time goes by we get more modern ideas, shall we say, and there comes a time when Bellamy's "Looking Backward" may be read without objection. Who decides when books should be taken off this list? If the minister wants a definite question, how many have been taken off this year, if any, or in the last forty years?
The list is revised from time to time. I cannot say how many books have been taken off, but that revision is kept up sufficiently, we believe, to meet the need.
I would not suppose that a publication declared immoral forty years ago, twenty years ago or even ten years ago would be declared moral today or tomorrow?
Certainly not.
A few years ago there was a good deal of controversy over "Bernard Clare" by James Farrell. I wonder if that book is still on the censored list? I merely use it as an example.
Yes, it is. I took the trouble to read it myself, and it is as filthy a thing as was ever printed.

I make no issue of that. I have never read it. I am well aware that the majority of hon. members are not interested in this subject, so I shall bring my remarks to a close. I might ask the minister one or two further questions which he can answer with yes or no. What is the system of examination of United States or for that matter any motion pictures coming from outside the country. Is that a provincial set-up?
That is a censorship which is undertaken by the different provinces.
And I assume the censorship of what goes over our public radio is a matter for the C.B.C.?
Yes; but I can say to the hon. gentleman that it is so pure it scarcely needs any censorship.

I think some of the hon. members to my right would not agree with that. Well, Mr. Chairman, I shall conclude my remarks by simply repeating what I said at first, that there is a sort of smugness about

this department of censorship which I do not like. In the first place I think the whole thing should be publicly aired; I think the department should take the public into its confidence. I believe the public should know the criteria by which books are judged. As far as I can see the minister has only two words, one of which is "good" and the other "bad". I do not think that is good enough for this day and age. I think the public should be taken into the minister's confidence as to the criteria by which these books are judged. I have no purpose in discussing this matter this evening except to obtain information for myself. I could read questions I have addressed to the department, and its replies. I have several returns which say this sort of thing "Answer to question No. 1: No. Answer to question No. 2: See answer to No. 1." I have several returns of that sort but I have never been able to get to the heart of this business of censorship.
I would say that the first step towards reform is a ventilation of the whole subject. In the second place-I should like you to notice this term in what I am about to say- the administration of censorship is beyond the scope and ability of the average customs officer. I believe this is constructive criticism. I do not think it is fair to ask a minister to wade through the books about which he has been talking. I do not believe any minister of the crown has time to do that sort of thing. There should be, in my opinion, a responsible officer with the experience, background, training and education which would make him, in the eyes of the public, a person fit to do that particular work. As his assistants, because I do not think it is fair to make any one official responsible, he should have a committee of people who know something about literature. They could be on a permanent basis if you like, but I would suggest a temporary basis.
The department should take the public into its confidence in this particular matter. The public should know by what criteria these literary works, if I may call them that, are adjudged. The principle must be known. You cannot have any censorship unless you have the support of the public, and without such criteria being known to the public, censorship can only be applied in a haphazard and discriminatory way.
I have just one observation, Mr. Chairman. Did I understand the minister to say that a book that might be considered immoral ten or twenty years ago would not, perhaps, be considered immoral today?

Not at all; I said the opposite.

Oh, I am glad the minister said that; because if that were what he did say, I would suggest that the book does not change. If our attitude towards it changes, that is different. It would mean that the attitude we took would be immoral, not the book.

300. General administration, $1,983,384.

I should like to ask the minister a question about some remarks he made in the house on November 25. At that time, the minister was speaking about permanent and temporary servants in his department. He indicated that there would be a reduction of some 4,000 in his department after the current fiscal year, because of the fact that the backlog upon which the department had been working would be finished. Will the minister say a word or two more about that?
I notice that this year the figure, presumably for staff, is up nearly $1,400,000. Perhaps the minister would indicate exactly why that was, and would say a word or two more about the impending reduction of these 4,000 people who, according to his statement on November 25, would no longer be needed after the end of this fiscal year.

I think it might be well if I made a short statement with reference to the departmental activity. In that statement, I shall cover the points which the hon. gentleman has made. In submitting the estimates of the taxation division of the Department of National Revenue, there are a few points which I should like to bring to the attention of hon. members.
You will have observed that by far the largest item in the estimates comes under the heading "salaries". The amounts needed to meet these requirements are greater than ever before. There are two main reasons for this: One, a substantial increase in staff; and two, the increases in rates of pay arising from the general over-all salary increases common to the public services as a whole since the war, and also the normal increases arising from promotion, reclassification of positions, and statutory increases within grades.
To deal with the first point requires a brief reference to the position of the department before the war. In the nine years ending in 1939, there were filed 3,590,224 personal returns and 253,903 corporation returns. Collections on all counts, personal and corporation, amounted to $833 million. In wartime, tax rates increased, exemptions decreased, the Excess Profits Tax Act was introduced, and
2818	HOUSE OF
Supply-National Revenue the federal government entered the succession duty field. As a result, there were filed for the nine years 1940 to 1948, 24,863,540 personal returns, 316,725 corporation returns. Collections for that period totalled $11 billion and $69 million on all counts.
Because of the pay-as-you-go system of collection adopted in 1942, a very considerable part of these moneys flowed in freely. But I think it is fair to say that, despite prodigious efforts to simplify procedures, the work of the division increased far beyond the capacity of the available staff. During the war, it was impossible to obtain the numbers of persons, men and women, especially in the skilled classifications, to keep the work on a current basis. In fact, many experienced men and women were lost to the services, and other war activities.
As hon. members know, a very serious backlog of work accumulated. At the end of the war, when staff became available, great efforts were made to recruit. To illustrate what happened, may I give you the following figures: On March 31, 1945, the staff numbered 6,421; it increased in 1946 to 7,097; in 1947, to 7,370; in 1948, to 10,478. The peak period was in March, 1949, when the staff totalled 11,704. Since that time, it has decreased and, as of October 31, 1949, it stood at 10,963.
Recruitment of course is but the beginning. Ours is a complex and difficult task, requiring that new employees be given extensive training, so that the full effects of the additional people were not immediately apparent. I am now happy to be able to advise you that, by the end of the current fiscal year, all returns filed in respect of 1948 and prior years will have been dealt with. To illustrate what has been accomplished, I should like to give you the production of assessments in this year. On October 31, 1948, we had 2,952,555 returns; from November 1, 1948, to October 31,	1949, we received 4,071,870
returns. The total was 7,024,425 returns. From November 1, 1948, to October 31, 1949, we assessed 5,868,677 returns, and the balance to be done between now and the end of March amounts to 1,155,748 returns. I can assure hon. members that the balance will be dealt with within the time limit indicated. I feel I should also add that it is my intention that all tax returns filed with my department will be dealt with without delay and, in any event, within twelve months of receipt.
To accomplish this gigantic task, it has been necessary to develop new procedures and new forms. The vast majority of individual taxpayers use the new form known as T.l short, introduced this year. Our


system now enables us to examine and assess practically all of these shortly after receipt. True, it is necessary to re-examine some returns and, as a result, it may be necessary to issue re-assessments. This is the point to which the hon. member for Eglinton referred last night. In all such cases, the re-assessments will be made within the year. There will be cases, of course, where taxpayers have deliberately falsified their returns. Where such returns are assessed without the true facts coming to light, the assessments will be subject to review at any time. Fortunately, it has been our experience that such returns comprise a small proportion of the total.
Because the work is now well in hand, and because it is at last possible to measure reasonably accurately the volume of future work, I am able to assure the committee that the decrease in staff evident in 1949 will be continued. It is expected that substantial reductions in numbers will be effected without major lay-offs, primarily because there is a large staff turnover and because, as the department is about thirty years old, there are members of the staff who are now reaching retirement age.

305. Maintenance and operation, $1,781,850.

Will the minister give us a brief outline of just what particular service this international short wave broadcasting station performs? What wave length in Canada on one's own radio can one pick up on the station? We are spending a lot of money on it, and personally I have never heard just what function it performs.

That makes up the $1,781,850.
I think it might be of interest if I gave the committee some information with reference to the international short wave service of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. On February 25, 1950, the international service of the C.B.C. will be five years old. In an inaugural broadcast Mr. Mackenzie King, who was then prime minister, said-and he was speaking to our troops overseas-
Tonight, Canada enters the world radio arena. As we undertake this new service, let us resolve that, in peace as in war, we will be true to the ideals you are so valiantly upholding-ideals which have made our country a nation. The unity of Canada belongs not only to Canada, it belongs to mankind. If we are true to ourselves, Canadian unity may well serve as a model for the wider unity of humanity. In the unity of mankind lies the one sure foundation of enduring peace.
The most powerful weapon against misunderstanding is the frank exchange of information among nations. This is a time when curtains of any kind, iron or otherwise, are tragic in the extreme when they exist between large groups of mankind.
The above facts provide the justification for the use by the nations of short wave broadcasting. Canada increasingly for the past forty years has found herself thrust out
Supply-National Revenue into the main current of world affairs. She could not if she wished pursue a policy of isolation. Our history and the traditional ties that result from it, and our geography which places us in a strategic position in the world have settled that for us. Increasingly Canada has been playing her full role in international affairs. It is, therefore, logical that she should have an international radio voice and that is exactly what the international service of the C.B.C. is.
Is this still in the quotation?

No, Mr. Mackenzie King's statement was brief.
Briefly the purpose of the international service of the C.B.C. is to project abroad as factually, honestly and simply as possible information concerning life in Canada which will help listeners in other countries to form a clear and accurate picture of what goes on here. It is a conscious attempt to place Canada before world listeners as a western democratic country. The voice of Canada, as it has come to be called, includes information concerning the simplest as well as the most complicated aspects of Canadian life. Through the co-operation of various departments of the government it speaks as authoritatively as possible of Canada's policies -within the safeguards, of course, of security. We tell our listeners about the way we live in our homes, the way we worship our God, the way we educate our children, the way we amuse ourselves, the way we conduct meetings and large industries, the way we elect political leaders and the way our machinery of government functions. In other words we are trying to present a picture of Canada as a vigorous democracy.
The international service is beamed daily to Europe in English, Norwegian, Swedish, Danish, Dutch, German, Czech, Slovak, French and Italian. It is beamed to Latin America daily in Spanish, Portuguese, French and English. It is beamed once weekly in English to Australia and New Zealand.
The response to the service has amazed even the most optimistic of its friends. Since its inception, between 125,000 and 130,000 letters have been received from individual listeners in various countries. Between January 1 and October 31 of this year 26,996 letters were received. These come from all types of people and all bear witness to a growing, lively interest in everything that is Canadian. They often ask for information concerning business, concerning labour conditions, concerning conditions under which they can emigrate to this country, concerning education and a thousand other aspects of the life and enterprises of Canada.

I thought it might be interesting if I read you a few excerpts from letters received by the C.B.C. international service. I have here some letters which were received recently from Czechoslovakia. You will understand how much such letters mean if you pause to remember for a moment the risks run by those who continue to correspond with us from that iron-curtain country. Our Czech mail used to be the largest. Since the coup in February, 1948 it has, of course, shrunk very much. We still continue to get a volume of mail, however, which compares most favourably with that received from that area by the B.B.C. and the "Voice of America".
I shall not take the time of the committee to read these letters. However they are from a great many people in these foreign countries who expressed their appreciation of the service rendered by the C.B.C. I have taken time to give some information about the international service, because there are about a hundred new members in the house who know very little about it. I presume they wonder why we spend a couple of million dollars a year to continue the service. It was for that reason that I have taken the time of the committee to give this information respecting a service which is non-revenue-producing, which is owned for all the people of Canada and which is used for the purpose of disseminating news about this country throughout the world in order that it may help those people who are behind the iron curtain, and give them some information with respect to this free democratic country, and to tell them something about the way in which we live. It is a service which I believe throughout the years will pay back big dividends, perhaps not in dollars and cents, but if we can attract to this country people who will become good citizens in future years, the money spent for the international short wave service has been money well spent.

Mr. Chairman, I am glad the minister did make the statement, because unless the older members of the house had served on the radio committee and followed this matter through since its inception, they would not know very much about what had taken place in this field.
I know of course that all hon. members support the international service and are glad to have the information the minister has just given. I do not see any other item in which the C.B.C. as such is provided for. I would say to the minister, and not in a critical way, that the service rendered by C.B.C. stations in the maritime provinces leaves much to be desired-and this is not because of any

inefficiency on the part of the organization as such. In my view it is due to the way the wave lengths are allocated in those provinces.
Only a little more than a year ago a station was established in the city of Sydney. I live within thirteen miles of it, but cannot receive its signals. It is on a wave length that is not found on the average Canadian radio, and its signals are jammed in with those of American stations. While the national programs are carried by the station, you cannot get them when you are within even a few miles of it. The wave length is not found on the average Canadian radio band, situated as it is away over about 1700 kilocycles. That is in among the American stations.
I have received many complaints about it, and I am mentioning it to the minister so that it may be checked up. I do not live far from Sackville, at which point a powerful station is located; but I cannot receive it, either. The signals from the Sydney station cannot be received in Halifax, three hundred miles away. The Cape Breton stations are received only very poorly. On the other hant the privately-owned station in Prince Edward Island can be heard in practically any par: of the province.
It seems to me the officials of the C.B.C. should discuss this matter of how wave lengths in the maritime provinces are arranged. I know that, in Nova Scotia particularly, the privately-operated stations are heard more clearly because of their better situation as to wave lengths.

The situation to which the hon. member has referred has developed because there was no other wave length available when the station was set up. While we are not discussing the C.B.C. execpt as it relates to the international short wave station which is managed by it, I would point out that representations have been made with respect to the whole matter of radio broadcasting to the Massey commission which is now sitting. I presume that some time next summer there will be a report from that commission suggesting changes that should be made for the betterment of the management of C.B.C.
Is it not expected that the report will be ready before next summer? I was hoping that it would be earlier because we expect a committee on the C.B.C. next session.

It would have been most helpful to the committee when discussing these items to have had before it the annual report of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. The year of the corporation corresponds to

the government fiscal year and that report should have been available long ago. Ii would have shortened the proceedings before the committee and would have obviated the asking of certain questions concerning the work of the corporation. When will that report be available? In the past the report has usually been made available by the summer, but here we are in December and it has not yet been distributed.
I am informed that the report is at the printers.
When was it sent there? Why was it not available long before this?
I cannot answer that question.

I have just one word to say about reports. I think all hon. members are anxious to conserve time in the review of the estimates. It would save a great deal of time and avoid the necessity of asking questions if these reports were available.
We did not have his annual report when we were considering the estimates of the Department of the Secretary of State last week, but the following day or the next day after the estimates had been dealt with the report came to us. Last Saturday we reviewed the estimates of the Department of Labour without having the report of that department before us, and on Monday or Tuesday of this week the report was distributed. There was more than coincidence in that, I am sure.
We are now dealing with the item pertaining to broadcasting and are told that the report of the corporation for the year ended March 31, 1949, a year that closed more than eight months ago, is still at the printers. I should like to ask for any possible explanation for the delay in providing these reports to hon. members. With the house sitting in the fall surely it was the minimum duty of the government to do everything possible to expedite the distribution of these reports. I say it is lamentable that there has been such a sparse and tardy distribution of important reports. Lacking this particular report it has been necessary for some hon. members to ask questions about this international short wave station. That information would have been available in the report.
I should like to say a brief word about the relationship of the house to some features of broadcasting. I do not intend to go into the question at length, but I do want to say that I think it most unfortunate that a committee of the house on radio broadcasting has not been set up for two years. In the 1948 session there seemed to be good reasons for not setting up the committee because at the close of the 1947 session we had just completed an
Supply-National Revenue extended review of all the problems relating to broadcasting in Canada. In the early part of that session we were not aware that certain important moves on the part of the C.B.C. were under way. For instance, had it been known in the 1948 session that a large purchase of property in Montreal was contemplated, a strong request would have been made by the official opposition for the establishment of such a committee in order that that purchase might be considered before any commitment was made.
During the first session this year three requests were made by the official opposition for the appointment of a special committee on radio broadcasting. At first the minister was noncommittal and he simply indicated that the matter would be considered. Then when my leader pressed for the appointment of a committee a resolution was placed on the order paper, but with the summary dissolution that followed the resolution died on the order paper, and the committee was not appointed.
There is a great backlog of work for such a committee to do. This has been a short session and it has not been feasible to appoint a committee to carry on an extended review, but regardless of whether the royal commission headed by the Right Hon. Vincent Massey has completed its work or not, I submit that early in the next session a special committee on radio broadcasting must be appointed.
You won't get it.

If for no other reason I think the subject of television should be considered of sufficient importance to require the appointment of such a committee. A study of that subject is urgent and essential. This country is losing valuable time. We should have been acting long before this.
The policy of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, to which the government is a party, has been one of dog in the manger. There were Canadian groups prepared to undertake the development of television at their own risk and expense, but through the control it exercises the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation would not permit them to do that. The corporation may not have been responsible for that decision, and it may have been the responsibility of the government. When the government finally did make up its mind about the middle of the first session of this year and announced that they were proposing a loan of $4 million to the C.B.C. to permit that corporation to undertake the development of three television stations, two in Montreal and one in Toronto, I am sure some of us wondered how the Minister of Trade

Supply-National Revenue and Commerce could have given his blessing to that proposal. When this matter was under consideration earlier this year the Minister of Trade and Commerce was one of those who said that such an expenditure would benefit only the residents of the metropolitan areas of Montreal and Toronto. In fact, the minister is reported to have said this:
If private operators think it worthwhile to risk their money, let them go ahead. Some of them, like Canadian Marconi, can hope to get it back by selling television sets. If I were living in my own town of Port Arthur I'd kick like a steer at paying taxes to bring television to Montreal and Toronto.
However, for some reason or other it became the policy of the government about the middle of the first session of this year to lend $4 million to the C.B.C. to develop three stations in the field of television.
I do not believe television in Canada ought to be a government monopoly. In the second place, I do not think it fair that the taxpayers of this country should be burdened with the cost of providing television on a basis which will benefit only the people in the metropolitan areas of Montreal and Toronto. When people who are capable of undertaking such a development are willing to risk their own money in it, without cost to the people of Canada, for the life of me I cannot see any sense or logic in denying them that opportunity, providing always- and there is general agreement on this-that the public interest is protected.
I am not going further tonight into this whole question of whether the C.B.C. ought to be permitted to continue as both competitor and regulator or, as it has been put in this house before, as judge and policeman as well as a party to the cause before it. I hope that very early in the next session an opportunity will be afforded parliament to undertake, by means of a committee, a study of this and of many other questions that have been developing since the last special committee of this house on radio broadcasting sat. It seems to me that is a matter of the highest importance. One might have hoped that the report of the Massey commission would be available early next session. If that should not prove possible, however, I submit that the House of Commons cannot wait. These questions I have referred to, particularly the matter of television, are much too important to be left in abeyance any longer.

I do not intend to oppose this item for the international radio service, though I am far removed from the metropolitan areas that have been referred to, which benefit from very lavish expenditures

made through the C.B.C. in respect to such fancy things as television. I do want to remind the minister, however, that northern Ontario has been badly neglected by the C.B.C. with respect to radio service. Vast areas in that part of the country are receiving no benefits whatever from the payment of their licence fees, nor are they getting any service from the C.B.C. or the government. If from its revenues the broadcasting corporation cannot look after those sections which are rather sparsely populated, and which were assured of service in the Aird report which was the basis for the development of the C.B.C., then the time is coming when these more remote areas will have to vigorously insist that no more money be channelled through the C.B.C. for such fancy things as television and an international radio service.
I would hope the minister might be able to give us some assurance that if the C.B.C. cannot find the money to provide this service, some other funds might be provided through his department or the Department of Transport to meet the cost of providing repeater stations in northern Ontario. Practically all the pockets of population in that area are on the transcontinental railway lines. These railway lines have telegraph lines which carry practically all the programs to western Canada, and those programs should be tapped for the benefit of these areas. If the C.B.C. is not prepared to do that, as they say they are not-and they have been resisting our requests for many years-I think a general vote of this house should provide for radio service in that part of the country, as was promised years ago when the conception of public ownership was first developed. At that time it was said that unless there was public ownership alongside private ownership, only in the highly commercial areas would we have adequate service.

I should like to join with the hon. member for Eglinton in expressing the hope that a radio committee will be established early next year, but perhaps from a different point of view. I know we cannot discuss radio broadcasting under this item, but I do want to say I think the radio committee should be appointed in order that the people of Canada may get a proper perspective regarding the corporation, the work the international broadcasting station is doing, and the work of the C.B.C. in general across the country. When I look back over the years I often look at the members of the official opposition and recall the speeches made by the late Right Hon.

R. B. Bennett. He would not have agreed with the opinions expressed tonight by the hon. member for Eglinton.
How do you know that? This is a different day and age.
I have read his speeches.
But that is all on ice now.
If the hon. member wants to make a speech, let him do so. I am just referring-
I am just checking up on you.

I would prefer that to be done by someone who can check up, rather than merely interrupt. It seems to me this committee should be set up in order that the public may be informed as to the services rendered by the broadcasting corporation and the extent to which that corporation has permitted private stations to contravene the broadcasting act and the regulations as approved both by the corporation and by parliament. As far as the stations in this country are concerned today, I think the people are getting thoroughly tired of the amount of soap and other advertising that goes on hour after hour, and the spot announcements that interrupt the programs every few minutes. I think we should look into the revenues of these private stations again, to see what they are actually making out of the monopoly the country grants them by way of wave length, because the possession of a wave length is the only monopoly there is in connection with radio. No one else can use a wave length that has been granted to a private station; therefore that station is given a monopoly.
It is said that these stations are operating without cost to the public, but in fact the cost is enormous when you consider the amounts people pay the advertisers for their products, against which the cost of broadcast advertising is of course charged. I think, too, the committee should go into the question. of television, because that can be both a benefit and a menace, particularly to the small businessman and the small manufacturer in the country. The cost of television programs will be tremendous, and the propaganda and advertising effect of the programs going into the homes of the people can be tremendous as well. If hon. members would just think it through they would realize the extent to which monopolies could be built up in our country through this great new facility.
As far as the international service is concerned, I believe the station and the expenditures on that station have been justified as
Supply-National Revenue the years have gone by. It is good, I think, that a powerful station in North America, and in one of the smaller countries such as Canada, if I may use that term, should be able to speak to the people of Europe who are not able to get information from the outside world and who can enjoy the programs that are transmitted across the iron curtain from one of the democratic countries which is not a great power, and therefore has no axe to grind, as might be the case with a great power. However, I do not want to go into the question of radio broadcasting tonight. I do think, however, there should be a committee set up to consider broadcasting in general, and particularly to find out why the C.B.C. has departed from the act, for example, in establishing private stations of 50,000 watts power. This was never contemplated by parliament at the time the act was passed. I believe a local community station can perform a local service, but I do not think it should be allowed to obtain a coverage that can blot out many of the other community stations, and interfere with the very basis of our broadcasting act.
I am anxious to look into one or two of these features critically, to ascertain why it is that the regulations and the act have been varied by the broadcasting corporation in cases of that kind.
Are the staff or the performers of the international short wave broadcasting station being screened by the R.C.M.P. at the present time?
Yes, they are.
Can the minister tell us how many of the members of the staff or performers are at present not actively engaged until that screening has been completed?
They are all active.

Is it not correct that the screening which is taking place is being conducted in connection with a suggestion that there has been certain broadcasting conveyed to European countries, which was not in accordance with the purpose of setting up this station?
I am informed that the answer is no.
Do I understand that one who has been commissioned to read a talk over the short wave broadcasting station is being screened?

The answer to the hon. gentleman's question, Mr. Chairman, is that the topic and the script are screened most carefully. In some instances, the person who is

The minister said that the performers are being screened. Those who are taking part in the programs are not in any confidential position. Where is the screening going to stop? Who screens the screeners?

May I ask the minister if a further appropriation will be made for school broadcasts in British Columbia? That service has been doing wonderful work in the rural areas, particularly in northern British Columbia. I understand some money is provided for that?
That question is entirely out of order, Mr. Chairman. We are not dealing with the C.B.C. at all, except in so far as they manage this international short wave station.

I want to know more about this screening. Who is being screened, and by whom are they being screened? What is the purpose in it? Is a person who sings over the air one who must be screened? Is there some mysterious inflection in the voice, or what is it?
The permanent members of the staff are being screened.
Not all those who are participating in programs?
No; I would point out that there would be no object in screening somebody who was playing the violin.

Are the
members of the staff regarded as being in a confidential position? Let us say an engineer; is he in a confidential position?
Except for the head of the division and his assistants, they are not in confidence.

I believe this should be clarified somewhat. It is obvious that there would be no occasion to screen violin players, acting as violin players, or shall we say a piper. But it is quite obvious that the screening was not directed to that. There would be a particular group who would be screened under circumstances of this kind, and I believe the minister is aware there is a particular group being screened. It consists of those who are making broadcasts by voice, and who are in a position to convey information to countries beyond the iron curtain. I do not think the minister will question the fact that there has been screening going on in regard to
[Mr. McCann.l

that for some time. Has the minister received an interim report, or any kind of report in regard to what has been found?
No, I have had no report at all. In any event, the report would not come to me.

There is no mystery about this. The minister has admitted that screening has been going on for some time. Those who are broadcasting by voice are being screened because of the fact they are in a position to communicate messages to areas that are not regarded as areas to which we would want certain messages to go. If the screening has been continuing for some time, as the minister has stated, then it seems that by now there should be some report, unless those who are under examination are not broadcasting.

The report, in the first instance, would be made to the chairman of the board of governors of the C.B.C. and the general manager. To date, there has been no report that would call for any positive action.

Item agreed to.
International short wave broadcasting station-
306. Acquisition and alteration; equipment, land and structures, including supervision, $971,250.

This item deals with the same subject, but I do want to point out why it is essential that a committee on broadcasting be set up at the beginning of the next session. In the earlier session this year, I received an assurance that that would be done. During this session we have not pressed the matter because of a statement that was made that this was regarded, although a session of a new parliament, largely as a continuation of the session that started last spring.
What has just been admitted is an indication of the reason why there should be a committee set up, and set up almost immediately after the next session begins, so that there can be an examination of this whole subject. In this case, $2,700,000 is being spent on this one operation under the direction of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. By the very nature of the activities it carries out, it could be a vehicle for the communication of messages which might be dangerous to the security of the state. The screening is being carried out, as has been admitted, with a recognition of that fact. It was only by questioning that this came out, and it was only by questioning at this moment that it was admitted there is some reason for screening in that particular case.
When I press for a report, it is stated that the report would not come to the minister, but would go to the chairman of the Cana-

dian Broadcasting Corporation. It is this uncertainty as to who has the information, when they get it-which was apparent in another case-that emphasizes the need for committees which can go to the root of the matter. A committee can ascertain what is being done in those branches of a department which, as agencies of government, are spending large sums of public money without direct supervision from any minister or deputy minister, but under direction of a public body. I can only repeat that because of what has been admitted now, with the admission on top of that, that the minister does not know what has happened in regard to screening that has been carried on for some time in regard to what could easily be an agency of highly improper activity, we see why it is so necessary that we start a complete examination of the whole activity of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation as soon as we meet in the next session.

Item agreed to.
Progress reported.
